utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, before we start this morning, I wonder if you could clarify something for me. Mr. Delic described himself as the deputy speaker of the Assembly. In other connections we received documents signed by him in which I have seen him described as deputy prime minister. What is the correct description of the position of which he holds?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is the deputy speaker of Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. When we --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we finished yesterday we had just been talking about the process in 1998 when you described how you went to Pristina and met with other VJ commanders and MUP commanders who were going to be involved in operations or actions related to the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism. I wanted to ask you about 1999, and I understand from your prior testimony in Milosevic that it was different in 1999. Is it correct that you did not go to Pristina in 1999 once the war started to get those kinds of instructions or orders about combat task; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In 1999 we did not go to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that's partly because of the circumstances with the war being on and it was difficult to travel, et cetera. So you received those orders either via telegram or telephonically or by courier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders came in either by courier or via the officers from the corps command, who with respect to issues such as corps control, would come into the brigade and some orders for other matters, short orders, arrived in the form of a telegram but encoded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back to the 1998 process that you described. These meetings in Pristina, where were they held, which building?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a meeting in the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had the impression from what you had said before that you had gone on more than one occasion. Is that not correct? I thought you had previously testified that you went at the beginning of each phase in which your units were going to be involved?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a total of two, at the most, three times, because my unit did not take part in all the phases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were all of those meetings, two or three, in the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that two of them were in the MUP building, but before I didn't go directly to that building, or rather, before that I would go to the corps command building to report to the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the meetings where the orders were passed out to you and your VJ and MUP colleagues, those were in the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was there at least twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at any of those meetings, was there anyone present who was not either VJ or MUP? Were there any civilians present at any of those meetings you attended in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were just the members of the army, and I knew most of them, and members of the MUP as well, and I knew just some of those individuals but I didn't know the majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to turn for a moment to a different topic and I'd like to go to Exhibit P1893. General, this is document that you wrote that in English has been translated as being referred to as a graduation thesis. I've got a hard copy I'll hand you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that in e-court this entire document has not been translated into English. There are three separate English translations for different parts. The first one I want to bring up is I think in e-court, it's the third one at the bottom of the list, which relates to the cover page and the index or table of contents section. If we can bring that one up first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you recognise that, I'm sure? Can you tell us yes if you do?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my graduation thesis, but I cannot see the purpose of discussing it here because it was discussed in 1997 when I discussed the graduation thesis and it was debated at a competent level when I was there to defend it. So I don't see the reason for bringing it up, but I am ready to acknowledge that it is indeed my graduation thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to worry about that. We're not going to test you or anything. I'm just inquiring -- I just want to inquire about some of the information contained therein, but can you give us a little background, first of all, about the School of National Defence, can you explain what that is and what was your purpose in attending in 1997. Can you give us a little brief background about that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The School of National Defence in the Republic of Yugoslavia was the same in any other country. Every state and army has a top-level school, so that the School of National Defence in my country at that time was the highest military school, and it provided a level of education which was equated to a doctor of science level. And officers attended that school who otherwise occupied the most important positions in the army, top-level posts, first of all with command responsibilities and those people who, if I can put it this way, who led the cadres service were seen as candidates for the top-most posts later on in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long is the programme? Is it a year? Six months?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I attended, the school lasted for one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who selects the candidates?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the superior commanders. In my case it was probably the corps commander. He put names forward to the army commander, and then the army commander to the Chief of the General Staff. But before that, certain conditions had to be met, candidates had to have had certain conditions met in previous schools in the military academy. You had to have a level of marks, an average mark, which was to be 800, so a mark of 8. And also during your service you had to gain high qualifications, particular distinctions, and at least as regards the last marks that you received. And then the candidate would write a request to be accepted and then there was an entrance exam that we had to go to Belgrade to sit for, and then those who passed the entrance exam would -- well, later on the corps commander and the commander at the level of the army gave their views on the entrance exam, and the staff of the -- expert staff of the General Staff would meet. And when the list of all the candidates was received, they would discuss which candidates they would send on for further training and education to the school. This also depended on the needs and requirements of the army itself, because there was a set number of candidates from the different branches and services. I was in the infantry, for example, and I think in my generation you could just have five candidates from the infantry. And then from the artillery there was a certain number of candidates to be put forward, then from the armoured and mechanised units another number, and as far as the services is concerned there was just one candidates, for example, from the quartermaster service, and also from some of the other services every second or third generation would put forward just one candidate. So care was taken, great attention was paid, to seeing that all the branches and services were represented adequately, and this corresponded to the commanding officers and the officers in the services and the army in general. Now, after the General Staff collegium reached its decision, the candidates were informed if they had passed or not, and that's how I was informed that I had been accepted and that I should report on the 2nd of September, 1996, to start my schooling there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My impression from what you said and what I read led me to believe that this is rather special, this is an honour, there aren't that many positions, it's highly competitive. Is that correct, my impression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is highly competitive, entrance to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many were in the class?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my generation, there were 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your thesis is the subject is translated into English as: "The Preparations and Engagement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Defence Forces to Prevent and Quell the Armed Rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija." How was your thesis chosen? Did you do that on your own or in consultation or was it assigned to you? How was that accomplished?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the school several topics were offered up, or rather, between 50 and 60 subjects, and one of those subjects was this one here; and I chose this subject because I had already done service in Kosovo and Metohija. And at the time there was just one other candidate from Kosovo and Metohija, from the units from Kosovo and Metohija, who was attending the school. So I selected this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the teaching counsel to approve my choice, to allow me to do the subject, and as you can see in my graduation thesis the teaching counsel approved it and the thesis -- approved the thesis according to which I wrote my topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And upon completing your thesis, once you finished writing it, what's the process? What happens next? Do you present it to anyone?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While writing a graduation thesis, and as you can see here I had a mentor, General Vukadinovic, a leader, and I would go to him for professional assistance and he followed my work generally. He was a sort of tutor. And as I'd finished each section, I would hand him the sections to review and to give his views and make his suggestions. And at the end - and this was already in 1997 - I defended my graduation thesis sitting before a commission of teachers from the School of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that sitting, how long does that take and what happens at the end of that process? Do you pass or fail? What becomes of your thesis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope there's a particular purpose to this, Mr. Hannis, because it seems an awfully detailed exploration of something which I think is probably consistent with common practice in many places of study.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're probably right, Your Honour. I may be spending too much time on that. If I get the answer to this question, then I'll move to some of the substance of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, after the sitting can you tell us what happens to your thesis? Is it published? Is it circulated?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having defended my thesis - and this is before a commission and the commission gives its assessment of the work, and my thesis got a mark of 9, it was marked with a 9 - normally it is not published afterwards; it's more for tuition purposes, for purposes of the school and further teaching and viewing the degree of capacitation for each candidate, how far each candidate was capable of writing a thesis like that and presenting his views on a set subject. And it remains in the school library, that's where it stays. It's not made public or published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The commission that you sat before, who was on that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the commission was Colonel Petrovic. He was otherwise the chief of the chair or department for operatics in the School of National Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or operations. There were two other members here, I can't remember who they were, they were also from the School of National Defence, and my tutor was there too, and there was General Vukadinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to go to the first part of the English translation. And, General, in your hard copy it will be -- it's page number 8, it's section 1.2 about the demographic structure of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In e-court the B/C/S page is page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, could you read the first two lines of that paragraph. I want to be sure the translation I have is accurate, and then I have a question for you about that, the first two sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In Kosovo and Metohija, the mother country of the Serbian people, the ethnic space of Serbs was continually reduced in the past centuries by the systematic advance of the Albanians from the neighbouring Albania and the expulsion of the Serbian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In past decades, the process culminated in a phenomenon unique in Europe, whose goal is through biological expansion and biological demographic based on a high birth rate among the Siptars to expel the population -- the Serb peoples."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to read that again. There seems to be a problem with translation. Could you read that second sentence again: "In the past decade ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In past decades the process culminated in a phenomenon unique in Europe, whose goal is to expel the remaining Serbian population through biological (demographic) expansion based on a high birth-rate among Siptars who would thus take over the ancient Serb lands."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, what was your source of information for claiming that it was the goal to expel the remaining Serbian population from Kosovo by this high birth-rate among the Siptars? What did you base that on?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you looked at the end of my graduation thesis, there are a hundred sources quoted there that I used in writing my thesis, and I think you should know that I myself was born in Kosovo and Metohija, that I lived there. I lived there until I graduated from secondary school. So everything I wrote there and read out is nothing knew. It's something that everybody knew about if they knew about the history of the Balkans, and especially the history of Yugoslavia and the history of the Serb people. As far as I can see, you -- oh, yes, there is the population, number of inhabitants. You see here that it says, or rather, it says 60 sources are mentioned here, the ones that I used in writing this book, or rather, this graduation thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that list at the end of your thesis, but can you tell me which of those specifically you relied on for this claim that the high birth-rate among the Siptars had the goal of expelling the remaining Serb population from Kosovo. Isn't it possible that they just liked to have a lot of children and there was no nefarious goal of expelling their neighbours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Albania, that's where their compatriots live, that is to say the Albanians of Kosovo and Metohija have their compatriots in Albania, and there, in Albania, the birth-rate is far lower. And I lived in Kosovo and Metohija myself, and I personally experienced the fact that in my village, which used to be a purely Serb village at one time, people suffered a lot of unpleasantness and had to leave. They had to leave the territory, to sell up their land, or even to leave their land behind, and to move out and go to Serbia. So that is a fact. It's a fact that is so well-known and so present in our lives that I see no real need to explain it further. It is true that they have a very high birth-rate. Do you want me to give you a specific example from my experience and in practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, let me --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If need be, I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on. I have another question to follow-up, it's page 3 of the English, and, General, I think it would be one, two, three pages on for you. It's underneath the chart about the demographic structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, in the e-court system it would appear that not one single page has been translated, but now Mr. Hannis has informed us that he has selected the translations, but unfortunately on our system of e-court we can't find the translations of the portions that Mr. Hannis is quoting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean the English is not available to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on my screen, why should that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the system we just have in B/C/S. We have on our middle screens, but in the system we haven't got any translated page, and also the problem is we have -- my learned friend mentioned that he just partially translated this document, but actually our request would be for the whole document, translation for the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would you make that request?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is one document, and if we just struggle pieces from that document we will lose the gist of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that our general policy towards documents resembling books - and this is like a book - is to expect translation only of the relevant parts. There's nothing to stop you if you feel it would help us inviting us to look at other parts and arranging for them to be translated if you've been taken unawares by this. But this document's in the unusual -- well, not necessarily unusual position, it's in the fairly common position in this trial that it's all in B/C/S, so therefore the language presents no problem to you or any of the accused, and you would have to spot for us problems we will have if we don't have English more than the particular parts which have been translated. So that's a matter for you to reflect on and suggest how it ought to be dealt with if there's a specific issue. So far as making available to you the English translation at the moment, Mr. Haider can tell me whether there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You still don't have the English pages? There is no reason, I'm told, why you should not have them available to you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do have on my screen, middle screen, but in the system, e-court system, there is no translation in English, just the document in B/C/S. That is the technical issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How then does it get on the screen if it's not in the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As I see on the monitor of my assistant, I see just B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We will discuss it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can discuss it with Mr. Hannis and work out a solution. We will continue since you do have it on your screen in English. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, the paragraph under the chart near the middle, after the reference to 1968, let me read this sentence and ask you a question. It's translated as: "Furthermore, in the entire post-war period, there was the planned policy of high birth-rate among Siptars in Kosovo and Metohija, motivated primarily by national interests." Can you tell me specifically who or what was your source for this statement that there was a planned policy of a high birth-rate among the Siptars? Isn't that just an assumption that you've made from the fact that there was a high birth-rate?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you were to read this right from the start, if you were to read the whole passage, what it says there right beneath the table, you would see what my sources were. One of the sources for the first part was the book: "Kosovo: Counter-Revolution that is going on." Another source I used for this data here is: The ethnic composition of Kosovo and Serbia in the -- in Yugoslavia, issued by a publishing house in 1993. So you would see these were not just my claims, but by writing them down here I accept them as my own. Because the policy towards the Siptar population, it was a special policy in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and this policy did not apply to any other ethnic minority. You have to be aware of the fact that after the Second World War the communists prohibited the Serbs from returning to Kosovo and Metohija, the return of those Serbs who had fled Kosovo in the Second World War because of the terror of the Kosovo fascists, because those fascists held the territory of Kosovo and Metohija together with the German and the Italian fascists, and they expelled the majority of the Serbian population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Mr. Delic. Mr. Hannis, unless you think this is helpful to the case and you want to hear all this, then I would prefer to have the matter dealt with differently. But if you want Mr. Delic to continue with these very, very long answers, exhausting the limited time you have when they don't seem to be leading anywhere, then that's a matter for you. The simple question here is: Where did he get the idea that there was a plan. Now, he's given us sources but they're no use to us. We want to know what is the basis in the sources for that plan, and I imagine that's what you want to know as well. So can we concentrate on what really matters here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would just like to interrupt, sorry, to make mention of certain historical opinions coming from men like Huntington who wrote this book, "The Clash of Civilization" and so on. These are different opinions that the growth of population is because for one reason or the other and also for the movements of civilizations and populations. So I think we are quite aware of various theories coming from political scientists and experts and writers, and we appreciate those facts I think. And I don't think his thesis really pertained to mainly those reasons. These were really to prepare for containing the terrorism in Metohija. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Part of my reason for pursuing this, Your Honour, has to do with arguing of bias and credibility of this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do want to follow-up a question on that, though. You do list as one of your sources for this section Vukasin Cerovic the book "Kosovo Counter-revolution in Progress." Is there anything in his book that points to an existence of a plan? Was there some document reflecting a meeting where this was discussed and agreed on? Is there some pronouncement by some member of the Kosovo Albanian leadership that this was a planned policy?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it appears rather ridiculous to me for somebody to make a plan to make more children. I support the argument that I presented in this thesis, is that there was a design, a policy that was implemented by stimulating more children, having more children, through child benefits that were given to employees, and it was a well-known fact that every child, every family that had more than nine children, the president would be the godfather of the ninth child, and that of course entailed certain privileges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The president of what would be the godfather of the ninth child?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all know who was the eternal president until the moment he died, Josip Broz Tito.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another section of your thesis, and this would be in the English part 2. And, General, it's page -- starting at page 72 in the hard copy, B/C/S in e-court is page 88. This talks about plans and preparations for prevention and elimination of a state of emergency. General, what were your sources for writing this section? Did you have access to secret military documents or plans?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a thesis, and right at the beginning it is stated that nothing of the documents that are relevant and current can be used; and this was not the subject of this thesis. If you were to look at the bottom of the page, it says there that Bosko Todorovic and Dusan Ilic wrote dissertation on emergency situation, and this book was published in Belgrade in 1989, it discusses the issue of plans. And as you can see here, everything is coached in terms of in principle. There should be plans at the level of the state, of the republics, of the provinces, of the municipalities, of the districts, and in all state organs and companies. I think this is something that is quite natural for every state. Plans should be in place for the elimination of certain crisis situations, disasters, natural or those that are a consequence of certain social events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should have asked you this question earlier, but I was slow to realize exactly what you were saying. Are you suggesting it was the Yugoslav state at that time that was encouraging the growth of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I have a question there as well that I'd like to follow-up on. Please tell me, the policy that was in place in relation to the benefits for more children and the matter of every ninth child being the godchild of your President Tito, was this confined to any particular ethnic group or could all ethnic groups benefit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not confined to any particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I need to follow-up on that. General, Judge Bonomy asked you if that was the policy of the Yugoslav state. That may have been the policy under Tito, but that was no longer the policy when Mr. Milosevic became president, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was no longer the policy, but at that time it became quite obvious that the number of Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija, if you were to look at the table, fell to 18 per cent, over -- in 1918 there were over 56 per cent, and when President Milosevic came into power as the president of Serbia, this figure was down to 16 or 18 per cent, I'm not sure. The problems that cropped up in the period that followed could not be dealt with simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I need to stop there.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- especially since the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia went into a crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You answered my question. Let me take you to page number 89 in your -- I think it's in your hard copy. It's page 105 of the B/C/S in e-court, page 17 of the English. Yes. And, General, if you could read the next-to-last paragraph for me because there's a question regarding the translation in my English. Could you read the first two sentences for us.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Furthermore, all the security organs and forces must be acquainted with the fact that all the procedures and measures they take are under direct surveillance of various quasi-humanitarian, democratic organizations, human rights organizations, and the public media. All the orders, statements, and actions, even if they're only formal in nature, must be in the spirit of the international law of war and in accordance with the -- and have to measure up with the criteria of the protection of the human rights and liberties."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The next section is defence forces -- number 8 is: Defence forces in Kosovo and Metohija available for the suppression of the armed insurgency. And if we could go to page 1 -- it's page 21 in the English. It's page number 93 for you, I believe, General, and page 109 in the B/C/S in e-court. And at the very top of the page talking about the civil protection and civil defence forces that are available. And in --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page did you say in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's page number 93, at the very bottom of the preceding page I think it has the title: "Civil defence and civil protection." And then here you list the forces available. Is it correct that in the end -- or in June 1997 or at the time you wrote this paper that the total number of civil protection and civil defence forces in Kosovo was about 2.000 personnel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already noted that this thesis was not done on the basis of the actual data. I could not put in the data about the units, but as far as I can see it says here 2.000 people. I don't know whether this was a typo. Maybe it should be 2.000 people because it should be indicated here the strength of the detachments in the versions 1 to 6. I think there is a mistake here and it should read 20.000 people. In fact, if you look at it, if you look at the bottom part, you will see that the first version has 230 people; then the second one, 184; the third one, 185; fifth -- fourth, 100; the fifth, 72; and the sixth 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you the sixth variant talks about 21 detachments, and I understand from the footnote that that's 50 people per detachment, which would come out to a total of 1.050. My rough math indicates that those totals are about 2.000. You have very precise numbers in the footnotes. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, I don't want to now start adding this up, you can do that during the break, but it's probably not 20.000 as you say. It may be about 3.000 people, that would be the total.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you must have got a mistranslation. I don't think I ever said 20.000. 2.000. It's about 2.000, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only the sixth variant envisages more than 2.000, but there are eight other detachments whose strength is different. I think that it would be about 3.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And the next part of your thesis, section 8.4, talks about the armed population, Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija who have not been given their assignments have been issued light infantry weapons with a single combat set of ammunition. Do you know when that issuance of weapons had been made to the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably in the late 1980s or maybe in the early 1990s, 1991. I don't know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by whom? Who had issued those weapons? Was it the army? Was it the Ministry of Defence? Who?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably -- that probably had to do with the Ministry of Defence, because later on these people were taken care of by the defence department that was in charge of the civil defence and civilian protection. Those weapons were those who had already been -- which had already been decommissioned in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you describe the particular kinds of weapons, which include some light machine-guns. The following paragraph you describe how they're organized, and measures had been taken to secure the villages and towns inhabited by Serbs. And in the next paragraph you say: "These forces numbered 16.000 armed people." Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was what I knew, because I inquired about that primarily in my own municipality and in other areas where I had people that I knew in the army; and that's how I reached this figure of about 16.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1997, when you wrote this, you indicated that if necessary, university students and third and fourth grade students in secondary schools of Serb and Montenegrin background, if they could be counted on, then the number would go even higher. My question is: You've made a distinction between civil defence and civil protection forces in section 8.3 and the armed population in 8.4. So that's something separate and distinction when you're considering the forces for defence in Kosovo and Metohija, right, the armed non-Siptar population is a distinction and separate group from civil protection and/or from civil defence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can get such an impression, but in the first part I talk about the units of civilian protection and civil defence, while the armed population had completely different tasks. They primarily were supposed to defend their own inhabited areas, while the civil defence and civilian protection units were tasked with protecting the civilian population in case of any kinds of threats, that was the civilian protection, and the civil defence were supposed to protect institutions, state organs, facilities, roads, and other vital facilities that are vital for any local self government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could Kosovo Albanians be members of the civil defence or the civil protection in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in Prizren, where I was serving, I was aware of those facts. There were many Muslims in particular, and in the municipality of Gora everybody was a member of the civilian protection and the civil defence and they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's make a distinction here, though. You talk about the Gora or the Gorani being Muslims, but those aren't the same ethnic group as the Kosovo Albanians, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Kosovo and Metohija there were four kinds of Muslims. Albanians were both Muslim and Catholic; there were Turks, it was an indigenous ethnic community that had come from Turkey and they retained their links with Turkey; there were Serb-speaking Muslims; and there were the Goranis. But in Prizren, in the civil defence and civilian protection units, all ethnic groups were represented in addition to the ones that I enumerated, there were also the Roma, Serbs, Montenegrins, absolutely all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The Serb-speaking Muslims, what ethnic group did they belong to? I'm not quite certain. You mentioned Serb-speaking, what does that mean precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In earlier history during the Ottoman Empire, the time of the Ottoman Empire those used to be Serbs of Muslim faith, they used to be Serbs and then they converted to the Islam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General, let's move to the -- I think it's your page number 115 in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English in e-court it's page 43, and in the B/C/S it's 132 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is section 9.4 that I want to ask you about entitled: "Involvement of the Serbian and Montenegrin population in the suppression of the insurgency." And I'll tell you in the preceding section, 9.3, you talk about how the civil defence and civil protection will be used or should be used in the suppression of armed insurgency. This section, paragraph 1, says that these forces can almost exclusively be used to carry out defensive task. Near the bottom of your page I think the first bullet point says: "They will protect the Serbian and Montenegrin population, mostly the old and infirm, women and children, so that the v/o," can you tell us what that means. Does that mean the men subject to military service? What does that abbreviation stand for?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means "vojni obveznici," men subject to military service or military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the armed Serbian and Montenegrin population will protect the Serbian and Montenegrin population, so that the men subject to military service in operational units won't have to be protecting their own families, correct, that was one of their jobs or task, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you almost always take things out of the context. In order to get a full picture of what item 9.4 discusses, you have to read the whole of it. It is true that in the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going on. I'm going to read the others -- at least a couple of the others. The next one -- and I think you have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have to go to the next page in e-court in B/C/S, still on 43 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Bullet point 2 says: "They will hold important areas and territories and infrastructional facilities ..." Number 3 is: "They will not allow the Siptar terrorists to gain control of a compact territory ..." And then after that third bullet point there's a new paragraph which says: "Units composed of the armed Serbian and Montenegrin population ... will be under the direct command of the competent military territorial command or VJ unit in whose zone they were located." How was that contemplated to work, whether they were going to be under the VJ or the military territory command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, this is what I thought, but you have to read the next passage too. "Efforts should always be made to have a military territorial unit, a MUP unit, or an operational VJ unit in the territory being secured by the armed Serbian and Montenegrin population."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And there are a number of other tasks listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the very bottom of that page in B/C/S, and in English we have to go to page 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, at the bottom of your page number 116, does it not say: "The armed Serbian and Montenegrin population will carry out these tasks in close collaboration with the other defence forces, primarily with the MUP and VJ units," right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What is in issue about this? There should be close cooperation with other defence forces in the first -- primarily with MUP and army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the reason I've been asking you about this is we'll talk about some of the Joint Command orders in 1999 a little later on today, but you recall, don't you, that in those orders there is regularly a standard phrase about the Pristina Corps with reinforced units and the armed non-Siptar population will engage in certain tasks. Do you recall seeing that or words to that effect in those Joint Command orders, making reference to use of the non -- of the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the orders, but I don't recall a single case when that armed population actually got an assignment in any of the paragraphs. The armed population never had any task, any assignment, to fulfil. Their only task was to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You do recall seeing that language in those orders, though, do you not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe in one order that I held in my hands. I remember there was some language to that effect, but I know that armed population never received an assignment, a mission. All armed units received their tasks, but the armed population does not because at the end of the day they are linked through Ministry of Defence sections in municipalities to the Ministry of Defence. And if they did receive any assignment, they could only receive it down that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then let's go to the next page, it's page 45 of the English, page 134 in e-court. It's page 117 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just, again -- I'm sorry to interrupt again --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but I thought we had just read that the armed Serbs and Montenegrins would be under the competent military command, either the military territorial detachment or VJ, and what Mr. Delic has just said is that they would all be linked through the Ministry of Defence. Now, that seems to be two inconsistent statements, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I said at the outset that it's ridiculous for a Tribunal at this level to review and discuss an academic thesis and compare it to the actual situation because I was forbidden in doing this thesis to use real names of units or any actual situation. All that I did through this dissertation, all the models of armed insurgency I developed myself, and this has nothing to do with reality. So to link what is written in my thesis with something that happened in 1998 or 1999 is, in my opinion, very, very wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be one thing, Mr. Delic, but there's also the question of our understanding of the terminology that's used in orders, which I think may be assisted by the way in which you have used similar terminology through your own experience in compiling this thesis. So we don't say it's valueless, but we do note what you say about its limitations. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this next section, section 10, on your page 117 and in e-court the B/C/S is page 134: "Exercise of command over the defence forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and Metohija in the context of the armed insurgency." And I need to go to the second half of the page and in quotation marks it says: "'The Yugoslav Army unifies all the participants in the armed warfare and exercise command over all of the defence forces in an area, zone, or territory where armed warfare is conducted at all levels, strategic, operational, and tactical.'" And there's a footnote to the: "Strategy of armed warfare, draft Belgrade, 1995." First of all, can you tell me what that footnoted item was, was that a working document from the army? Was that another thesis from the college? What was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategy of armed combat is one of the most important documents. It's true that this is a draft strategy, but it's one of the most important documents of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us who the author of that was?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such documents are usually authored by more than one person. This was written by a group of authors. The greatest connoisseurs of certain topics of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, in this case do you know was this authored by a group of active-duty VJ high-ranking personnel or was it written by civilians or who?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was written mainly by high-ranking officers with Ph.D.s, more than one, depending on the area in which they were experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that proposition stated there in quotation marks is really not inconsistent with the constitution and the provisions in the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army, is it, that in armed warfare the army is the one that is responsible overall for the defence of the country; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paper could not have been written if it ran counter to the law. Like any other document or rule of the army, it has primarily to be consistent with the Law on Defence and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next paragraph relates to something we just discussed a few minutes ago. It says: "The issue of unified command of the VJ, civil defence and civil protection units, and the armed Serbian and Montenegrin populations has been resolved in a satisfactory manner, since the commands of the VJ units liaise with these units through the organs (sectors and departments) of the Ministry of Defence." Is that correct? Is that how it was to work in 1997, everyone understood that the army would be the overall commander for those units in a state of armed warfare?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph that you read from the strategy is quite all right. It envisages that the army should unify all participants in armed combat; however, if you read on you will see which problems have to be dealt with from the legal and legislative point of view. So you have to read the next paragraph. I realized then that there is a problem with the armed combat, namely, the problem of legislating the various roles and responsibilities between various participants, including the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the MUP. And it says: "Despite the position of the armed warfare strategy and the unified command system quoted above, it had not been implemented in practice. Instead of a unified command of the two most important elements of the defence forces, we have only organized collaboration in the execution of their missions in the suppression of the armed insurgency." If you take only one sentence out of this paragraph, then you might be misled, but this is just my understanding, my thinking, my reasoning --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- based on certain rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next paragraph after the one I just read and above the one that you just quoted from partially, said: "The basic problem of the unified command as many in the context of the armed insurgency in Kosovo and Metohija is the legal delineation of competencies and responsibilities between the Serbian MUP forces and the VJ units." And that certainly is true, that was part of the problem in 1998 and 1999 before a state of war was declared, right, because there was a lack of clarity and legal precision about what MUP could do and should do and what the army could and should do in Kosovo during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. In peacetime, it's quite clear what the MUP is doing and what the army is doing. The problem that arose in war had to do with the resubordination, and it was only from that aspect that you could interpret, read, what is written here. If resubordination had really occurred, if this part of the strategy of armed warfare had been honoured, at least with regard to the MUP -- but then as far as civil protection and civil defence units are concerned, the relevant ministry should have issued its own directive on resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your thesis you make a proposal to address this problem, do you not? You talk about creating a command and control organ between the General Staff and the Pristina Corps command, right? We have a chart on page 47 of the English, page 136 in e-court, and I think it's between pages 118 and 119 of your hard copy. Can you explain to us, starting at the point below the VJ General Staff, that next box and the arrow down to Supreme Command [sic], can you explain what you put there and what your proposal is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My proposal was that from the General Staff a team should come to the Pristina Corps, and that team would be the forward organ, the forward command organ, under circumstances of armed insurgency. On the left you should see that from the 3rd Army a team should also come to command forces to suppress armed rebellion, and I also envisaged that another team should come from the staff of the MUP of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija to command MUP forces. And at the level of the Pristina Corps there would be a unified command over all forces in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. And from the command of the Pristina Corps, where all these teams would be based, the General Staff team, the 3rd Army team, and the MUP team, from that level command would be exercised over army units and MUP units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you used the expression an arrow pointing down to Supreme Command. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I did say "Supreme Command," I misspoke, Your Honour. I meant Pristina Corps command. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't realize I had said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And, General, I would suggest to you that during both 1998 and 1999 there was a body in existence to help deal with this problem of coordinating MUP and VJ activities in dealing with the armed insurgency, and that was the Joint Command. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on then, and I want to ask you about some of the -- we'll leave your thesis behind, and I want to ask you about some of the actions engaged in by your forces in 1998. Can we turn first of all to Exhibit P2067, if we could have that up on the screen. This is a document from you, signed and stamped. It's dated the 9th of March, 1999, and the title is order for engagement of forces to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the general area of Jeskovo village sector. Now, it's my understanding that this is an order that you issued based on an order that you had received either that day or the day before from General Lazarevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that order originate initially from him or did that order come to you after you had made a proposal to him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that was preceded by a report, and we have seen this report during examination-in-chief. It had come from security forces, saying that in villages of Jeskovo and Kabas terrorist forces were assembling, and I had similar reports from my brigade. After that I received a request from the corps command to propose a concept for executing that task. I sent them my ideas in the form of a telegram, the commander reviewed it, and then he wrote an order that was again sent by telegram. After that order, I coordinated with the local MUP and the secretariat in Prizren. I exchanged information about that location, and I coordinated that activity as I was ordered to. I planned which forces of the army to use, and the MUP people told me which MUP forces are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we coordinated exactly on which routes, which axes MUP forces would move, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a specific question about the document, if I may. General, at the top on the upper left-hand corner we see it's from the command of the 549th and it's dated the 9th of March, but one thing that seems to be missing that we see in other documents of this nature, there is no log-book number. Is that unusual or was that the practice in your brigade or can you explain why there's no number in connection with this order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When orders are concerned, there may and may not be a number. What's important is to indicate the unit, the day, and the location where the order was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what decides whether there will be a number given to a document like this or not? Is there not some uniform practice? We've seen a lot of very detailed protocols and procedures in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we also look at the instructions on staff affairs, we will see that a number may be given but at a level of a unit such as a brigade because I'm sending this order only to my units. This order is registered in my command, but that number where it says "command of the 549th Brigade" and a certain number along with it, it's usually on the back side of the order. Maybe if we scroll down to the end we will see it at the end. Sometimes that is stamped below my signature, sometimes on the flip side, but this order is written completely in conformity with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll look at the last page in a minute and see what's there. I wanted to go to the next page in English, and it's -- I'm looking for item 5.1. In the B/C/S I think it's on page 2 as well. And this is where you are citing unit task, and item 5.1 is a task for -- well, can you read it out for us because there's some question about the translation of what is in English as "CMS." Could you tell us what that CMS-1/549 is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A company of mixed composition. 1/549 brigade with a firing squad -- firing platoon, from the company of 1/1 with your own forces shall execute movement from the area of deployment along the axis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Tell me what these mixed composition companies are. First of all, in general, what is a mixed composition company? By the title of it I have an idea, but ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Companies of mixed company were formed after the arrival of the OSCE mission, and they were the units that were allowed to stay in the border belt. In total, as far as I know, there were nine such units, three of them outside the border belt and six within the border belt. As for my brigade, we were allowed four mixed companies, and the reference here is to that personnel. And they're called of mixed composition because they have both infantry, armour, artillery, and the necessary number -- or let me say a logistical unit, so they are independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us then at this time, in March 1999, the approximate composition of this particular mixed composition company. Approximately how many men and what was the combat equipment contained in this mixed company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for infantry, they had one motorised company that's around 150 men; they had a tank platoon with complete personnel, that's up to 15 men; they had a platoon of howitzers, 122-millimetres, with a complete crew it's up to 15 people; they had communications team, 10 to 15 people -- sorry, seven to eight people; and they had logistics, up to 15 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what vehicles did they have? Was there a tank? Were there any BOVs or APCs?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems my microphone is not on. Every company of mixed composition had one tank platoon, that's three tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about any other vehicles for the motorised company? How did they travel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of these mixed-composition companies had a certain number of ordinary vehicles, trucks for transporting men and materiel, and it differed from one company to the other. They were not able to transport all the people necessary in one go, but I can't give you figures. They had perhaps up to ten vehicles, different types of vehicles. Each had a water truck and a certain number of vehicles carrying ammunition. They would have a vehicle with food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they have any armoured vehicles? Did they have any BOVs or APCs, Pragas, or are you talking about just ordinary trucks?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the combat vehicles that each company had would be three tanks, one tank platoon, and as far as I remember, although you could see this -- well, perhaps one of these mixed-composition companies had a Praga platoon. But since I had a total of just one battery in the brigade, then they would come in only when absolutely necessary. My unit did not have any APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Item number 5.3 there is -- could you tell us what that is. The English translation is idc with a full banana over the c. Can you tell us what that abbreviation stands for?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an establishment unit from the brigade, the sabotage and reconnaissance company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And item 5.4, what is that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they're talking about is the light artillery rocket division of the PVO battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did the brigade then have some anti-aircraft defence resources of its own that you could command, that you didn't have to liaise with or get permission or coordination with the air force?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit, every combat unit, operative unit of a brigade rank had within its composition a unit which was intended for anti-aircraft combat. The motorised brigades had light artillery rocket artillery battalions, the PVO, anti-aircraft defence, that had a number of batteries in their composition. And they had a rocket battery, but these were rocket-launchers of the 2-M type, Strela 2-M type, and cannon batteries, the 20-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And items 5.6 or 5.7, there are tasks for the 37th PJP detachment and a task for the 5th, it looks like, PJP company of Prizren, right? So it appears that you are giving tasks to the police in this order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could do it that way, but it's not absolutely correct because I never issued orders to any police unit. However, I was in the police for coordination but not one of my commanders was. And each of my commanders had to know what the assignment was, the assignment of these two police units that took part in this particular assignment. And they had to know it in detail, so as to avoid friendly fire. Now, if you were to move on, you would see towards the end who this order was addressed to and then you will see that it was not addressed to any of these MUP units but just to my commanders. And when they receive this order, my commanders would have to prepare their units and to issue their own orders. And one of the basic things that they have to say to tell them is who their neighbours are on the left and on the right, or rather, for support unit who they are supporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, if we could move on to page 6 of the English and it's item 10 of the B/C/S. I don't know if that's on the last page or the next-to-the-last page. Yes, it's on the last page of the B/C/S. Here we have a section about the command and communications, and we see that the command composition includes yourself and then Lieutenant-Colonel Konjikovac. Was he your deputy or Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was my chief of the operations organ. The Chief of Staff during that time was along another axis. I'd just like to draw your attention, Mr. Hannis, to something I said earlier on when you asked me something at the beginning, and you see here it says the command of the 549th Brigade, it has the stamp, and it has the number at the end of the Serbian version underneath my signature you'll find the stamp, where it says how many copies and who was it was addressed to, who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's why you asked me at the beginning why it didn't have a number, you can see here that it does have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll going to come to that in a minute. Major Djokic was he a MUP guy or was he a VJ?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Major Djokic was also a major from my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you showed me where there is a stamp and it had a number, so is that the log-book number for this order, 1966-2?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll down --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need to scroll down. Sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand the numbering system, if there's a 1966-2, there must have been a prior document that got the number 1966-1 that would have referred to this same general topic. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1966-1 under that number would be the order of the corps commander, and it has its own number from the Pristina Corps. But when it reaches my brigade, then a stamp is placed on it and the number 1 is placed there. And what I write can have numbers 2, 3, 4, and onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that's the case here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me when this action was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This action was undertaken on the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the significance of the date 24th of May in the stamp where the number is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that -- as I say, that's when this order was recorded and logged in the brigade in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your last answer I understood then, the order you got from General Lazarevic would have received a number in your brigade in your log-book, and you think that's probably what got 1966-1?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that was the case. When you receive from the superior command an order which relates to a set situation, then it always has the number 1 on it; and anything you receive from the brigade is given the number 2, and if there are more than one document, then it can have the numbers 2, 3, 4, and so on. That's the usual method, and I assume that this was that case too, but as I didn't look at the actual log-book I can't claim for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We see that under your signature there's a list of three photocopies made and delivered to the mixed composition companies and to the organ for operations and training. And then at the bottom it also says: "Forces engaged from the barracks." Who would that be pertaining to? I see in item 5.6 for the 37th PJP Detachment it talks about moving from the barracks. Is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What is meant here is the reconnaissance company of the military police and the LRD, the PVO, anti-aircraft defence, and maybe some other unit, because -- I don't have that other page here, but it relates to the barracks. We had the military LARD company, the reconnaissance company, the light artillery rocket battalion, anti-aircraft defence, perhaps one of the rear units, logistics, all those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I don't see in this list then for whom copies are made any reference to the MUP. Did they not get a copy of this order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did not get a copy and there was no need for them to receive one because coordination with them had already taken place before this order was written. Their commander issued tasks and assignments to his own unit, so that in that respect I had no points in common or no links with them on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that earlier coordination had been done how, you meeting face-to-face with one or more people from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually the chief of the secretariat would do that. Here we see two units, the commander of the 37th Detachment and the commander of the 5th Company, where they specifically said which forces would be deployed, their own forces and the forces they have at their disposal. And then we divided up the line of blockade, which part of the line would be held by the police forces and which part of the line would be held by the army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General. Then I take it from that that you did have some face-to-face meeting with the police to get that information and work out those details, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that having received an order from my commander, I then came into contact with the chief of the secretariat and that he would set his -- have his commander and his komandir come in, and that in his office we would define coordination for this particular operation, and then I did what was necessary for my units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Delic, we need to break again. If you would please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall resume again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I'd like to show you P1998. This exhibit, General, is a sort of after-action report on the Jeskovo village action that was taken on the 11th of March. You've seen this document before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It's my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on the date in English it's written down as 12 March 1999, but on the B/C/S I can't tell, is that 12 or 22? It looks like there's been a handwritten change or correction. Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the action was conducted on the 11th of March, then most probably the number there is 12, the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this, the first paragraph, says: "On March 11th pursuant to the order of the 549th ..." And that's what we looked at before is, P2067, "to provide support to the MUP and to the approval by the Pristina Corps command," makes reference to their number 455-21 of 8 March, "the STS," Siptar terrorist forces, "were routed in the Jeskovo village." I want to ask you about a couple of matters in here. You know that since March 1998 that there was concern in the international community about what they viewed as the use of excessive force or disproportionate force in anti-terrorist operations. You knew about that, right, that there had been a UN resolution in March and another in September leading up to the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement? You knew that was a concern, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were referring to 1998, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's when it had begun by at least, in early 1998, and it continued throughout 1998 and into 1999, didn't it? The internationals were concerned about what they viewed or termed disproportionate force or excessive force in anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo. Did you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't agree with you. At the beginning of 1998, as far as the army units are concerned, all the army units were in their peacetime locations, in barracks, and apart from the almost daily incidents along the border there was nothing else right up to April, or rather, the units did not leave the barracks at all. There were regular activities going on. In the territory there were attacks from time to time on MUP forces and civilians along the communication lines or roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is your quarrel with me that I said from early 1998 instead of saying from March 1998; is that the problem?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first anti-terrorist actions were launched at the end of July 1998, when these Siptar terrorist forces had already taken control of 50 per cent of the territory. Up until then, apart from the attacks on the police and the attacks at the border, there were no, as you call them, excessive or disproportionate use of force, there was none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware of the incident at the Jashari compound in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you know that there was some complaint from the international community that they viewed that as an excessive or disproportionate use of force, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there. I do know that the compound of the Jashari family was not only in that year, but for years before that, a terrorist stronghold. And I, of course, regret that on that occasion -- it was an anti-terrorist operation launched by the MUP, and I regret that on that occasion women and children were killed; however, I was not there and don't know the details of what happened and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, it's important to listen to what's actually being asked of you. The rights and wrongs of that incident, and indeed any other, are not being explored in these questions. The question relates to international concern about what was happening in Serbia. Now, are you saying that you were not aware of United Nations resolutions in 1998 preceding the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement that expressed concern about the use of disproportionate force, whether they were well-founded or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Hannis used those resolutions and referred to them and wants to ask me something here in connection with them, I would certainly wish to have them in front of me as a document so that I could state my opinions about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you're not listening, with all due respect. You're being asked about your state of knowledge in 1998. Now, can you say whether or not you knew there was international concern about the alleged use of disproportionate force by Serb forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, that was in the second half of the year, perhaps the month of September; but at the beginning of the year I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, in July of 1998 had not the Pristina Corps commander, and I think you yourself, issued orders about not firing the heavy weapons, the artillery if there were internationals or foreign observers or foreign journalists in the area. There were such orders issued in July of 1998 by the VJ, correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such orders were issued; however, not in the sense in which you would like to present them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard answers from other witnesses, and the reason was that they didn't want to harm any of those people, but I suggest to you that an additional reason was because they knew the internationals had criticised -- the army was aware that the internationals had criticised the security forces for excessive and disproportionate force. And that was another reason for the issuance of those orders, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, when I wrote my order - and that is how I understood the order from my commander - the prime goal was that people from the international community who happened to be in those locations would not suffer losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Set aside the international concerns about disproportionate or excessive force. Isn't it true that in March of 1998 there was at least a local concern about the disproportionate or excessive use of force in anti-terrorist operations among the civilian population in Kosovo? You knew about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not precise in asking your question. What local population are you referring to? What local concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you an exhibit then. Can we look at 5D845.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That must have been a translation problem because the question was among the civilian population in Kosovo, which is a wider description.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll just continue on to the exhibit, Your Honour, and maybe I can do it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a report from the 549th dated the 9th of March, 1998, and you'll see under item number 1 the second sentence says: "The MUP forces in the territory of Drenica instilled a certain degree of fear among the local Siptar population." And that's a reference to the Jashari incident, incident it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go back now to Exhibit P1998. And, General, to remind you, this is the Jeskovo action and it's your post-event report to the Pristina Corps. And under item number 1, the second full paragraph, second sentence said: "We estimate the strength of the Siptar terrorist forces in this village was between 25 and 30 men."
