And in the next paragraph you indicate there were no civilians in the village. And in the following paragraph you say the Siptar terrorists attempted to breakthrough along a certain axis. Given the fact that they were encircled, this attempt to breakthrough failed. And then on the next page in English and still on the same page for you your estimate of terrorist losses was nine killed and no one was captured. Item number 2 talks about the forces of the VJ engaged, and we see there were seven -- about 611 army personnel and about 300 police personnel. So 911 men, six tanks, four anti-aircraft guns, three armoured vehicles, et cetera. I would suggest to you that this is an example of excessive or disproportionate force, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely wrong, and you will admit that I am quite familiar with these issues. When you say 900 personnel, it's not 900 men fighting, taking part in the actual fighting. A whole sector needs to be blocked. Blocking a sector means that you have to block several square kilometres of the territory. So I would agree with you if we were talking about 900 men fighting nine men, but only a small unit took part in the fighting and all the other people blocked the territory, lest the terrorists should be able to ex-filtrate from that territory. After all, you have to know that military principles, not only in our army but in the world, allow that if one is dealing with the terrorists that any force may be legitimately used. And our anti-terrorist units were taught on the best practices of the British SAS, the US seals, and the Israeli Musad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page for you, and in the third paragraph I think you'll see the amount of ammunition used, starting with 1.656, 7.62-millimetre bullets, and on up through the number of shells used in the heavier weapons. Regardless of how many men there were, isn't that a disproportionate amount of information -- of ammunition for nine Siptar terrorists?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we assumed that there were 30 terrorists there, not nine. If you read my order, right at the very beginning of the order it says that in the previous days another 50 were expected to have come in that area. So our estimates, our knowledge, was that there would be a much larger number of people. When we're talking about terrorists, this is definitely not excessive use of force, because if one is dealing with terrorists in other countries you can use the -- you can use armed helicopters, you can call in air force, and we never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, General, I did note that you had estimated 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you are dealing with a terrorist or combat force, there's surely a distinction between using overwhelming force and the excessive use of force. I wonder if we are, in fact, discussing each discussing the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on to another exhibit. This is in the same vein. I want to follow through on that and then I'll move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to show you Exhibit P2072, 2072. This is another order from you. This is to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Kabas village, and we have in evidence Exhibit P2071, which is the preceding order from the Pristina Corps number 455-34 of 16 March. Again, this is similar to your previous order that we saw, and we see again in items 5.8 and 5.9 a task for the police. And I want to note in item number 10, which is page 7 of the English and it's probably the last page of the B/C/S, you do have on this occasion MUP personnel listed as being -- as part of the command, the commander of the 37th PJP Detachment and the commander of the 5th Company. Do you recall, were they with you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were at the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this time your estimate was that there were about 60 terrorists located in the village that you were going to attack, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here in the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P1999, could we have next, is the post-action analysis prepared by you and sent to the Pristina Corps. It's dated the 18th of March, 1999. You'll see in item 1 that during the operation you estimated the strength was between 30 and 35 men, and in the following paragraph again you note there were no civilians in Kabas. And on the following page in the English, two paragraphs above item number 2, you said: "During the operation the Siptar terrorists did not drop their weapons or combat equipment until the last moment, when they changed into civilian clothes and attempted to breakthrough on a particular axis where they came across our unit in the blockade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with -- by your leave, on page 48, line 1, my colleague must have made a mistake and said "60 terrorists," whereas in the text it reads that there were 80, so just for the sake of clarity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The suggestion, Mr. Hannis, is that the P2072, the earlier document, notes anticipated 60 -- sorry, 80 terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was reading from the third paragraph where it says "about 60 terrorists are armed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can check that later. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He's correct it does say 80 in the first paragraph, in the third paragraph it says 60 of all those terrorists were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the last moment, these guys fled but they ran into the blockade. Your estimate of STS losses, 11 were killed, and again no one was captured. It also says in that same portion that: "During combat operations the inhabitants of Selograzde village, Grejkovce village, and Korisa village were seen moving in the direction of Suva Reka and Prizren. You were out there, weren't you. Can you tell us how many civilians were leaving the area during this operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not leave, since the area of the village of Korisa is outside of the blockade line and close by is a MUP check-point. The population was not permitted to leave to some other area but they were taken back to their village. As regards the village of Selograzde, it is at the foot of a mountain and it was not within the blockade line. It was, however, observed that the population in that village was getting ready to leave, but since the police and army units were moving away, not towards, that village, the population did not leave their territory. They remained there. So afterwards all of them came back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- under item number 2, the fourth paragraph explains before you set off to crush the Siptar terrorist forces you used civilian columns to bring secretly some forces to Sevce village. Did you do that? You put some of your forces in a civilian column and moved them to that location?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's a mistake. Civilian trucks. Those were the forces that had come from the other side of the mountain to block the village of Kabas, because that village was up in the mountains perhaps at about 700 metres above sea level. The forces that were coming in were supposed to move through an area that was at 2.000 metres and through very deep snow, a metre-deep snow, in order to be able to block the village from the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these civilians were moving through that snow during this operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're not talking about civilians here. These are soldiers, my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, but the earlier part of the report where you talked about the civilians moving in the direction of Suva Reka and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was little snow in that area and there was no snow on the roads at all, and I have already said that the civilians from those villages, the village of Korisa is on the road itself. The village of Selograzde is closer to Suva Reka. When the fighting started, it was observed that the population in those villages was milling about, but nobody left that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The fact is, General, that both of these operations that we just talked about in March, on March the 11th and this one on March the 17th, these were not defensive activities by the VJ. These were offensive actions initiated by you, and this was contrary to the provisions of the October agreements, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should have read the previous reports. In both locations attacks had already been launched from those sectors on my forces, forces that were stationed at the village of Jeskovo in the village of Zur in accordance with the agreement. If you read the beginning of the order, you will see that an attack had been carried out on the road and there was a direct attack on the forces that were there in accordance with the agreement. So you cannot tolerate the terrorist threat to the roads, their attacks on the units, without responding to those attacks, without neutralising those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but this is not a direct response to an attack happening at the moment; this is some days later, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that really means nothing. My commander received reports of the attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it may mean nothing, but is that correct in terms of timing, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an immediate response, an immediate response to an attack that was at that time, happening at that time, but it is a response to an attack that happened a few days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we heard evidence that in a VJ collegium session, I think on the 18th of March, it was discussed -- General Dimitrijevic I think in particular brought it up, they had a concern that they were being told from below, from the 3rd Army and from below, that the actions taken in Kosovo were defensive. And he had information that it was something different, as I say, like we've seen here, that it's being initiated by the VJ and not in direct response to an attack that's ongoing. Were you aware of that? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things that were happening at the collegium, that's not something that I know of. I had no way of knowing that, but these were fully legitimate actions, both the Jeskovo action and the Kabas action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me next ask you about one that takes place after -- after the war started, after the NATO bombing began. This is Exhibit P2002. This is a report of yours dated the 30th of March, 1999, signed and stamped --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We don't have any number on this at the beginning or, General, I would tell you, you can see in a minute on the last page it only has your signature and stamp but there's no report number or log-book number. It says: "Analysis of operations of the 549th to destroy Siptar terrorist groups in the area of Malisevo and Pagarusa." It sets forth that in the period of 30 March to 3 April, pursuant to an order by the commander of the 549th and to an -- and an order by the Pristina Corps number 455-90 of 28 March --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which I advise the court is Exhibit P1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- The STS was destroyed in the general area. One question I have here is: The date of this document is the 30th of March, but it says in the period 30 March to 3 April these activities were carried out. Can you explain how that is, that you're writing on the 30th of March about activities going through the 3rd of April. Is that just a typographical error in the upper left?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's obviously an error. I signed this document and it was actually drafted by my operations officer. At the time when this activity was going on, he was the commander of Combat Group 5 and he wrote this later. So this is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know, I am familiar with what is written here because I read it before I signed it, but I did not notice this mistake at the time because it was already April by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was your operations officer who drafted this, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Lieutenant-Colonel Stojan Konjikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're still on the first page I would ask you to read the second paragraph under the big one in the middle. It said: "The organization of the defence was partly characterized by the fact that the refugee population from the general area of Retimlje was present in this area, concentrated in the Banja village sector." There were several thousand refugees in that area at the time, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this activity is the continuation of the activity of the 25th, when it was determined that the Studencane, Dobrodeljane, Pagarusa axis was used to move the population out from the previous zone. I was there during the activity, I was present, and I saw that the population was moving in one direction towards Belanica, from the villages of Kravoserija and so on, Pagarusa, and from the villages that were closer to where I was, the population moved on to the road that was used by the army at that time for its own movement. I noticed the population myself; I couldn't tell their number, but the civilian population was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple of paragraphs down it says the Siptar terrorists did not abandon weapons and combat equipment during the battle until the decisive moment, when they withdrew dressed in civilian clothes and tried to blend in with the stream of fleeing civilians." We're talking about thousands of civilians trying to leave the area, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians were moving in two directions, as I already said, towards Belanica and down the asphalt road leading to the village of Ostrozub.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many, if you know? We are talking about thousands, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think further down in this document there is an estimate as to the number of those people, but this part that was moving towards me on the asphalt road, I think that was between Dragobilje and Moralija, those two villages. Their number could be a few thousand. Now, as for Belanica, there were more of them, but when we completed our part of this activity, we did not move towards Belanica. I think that on the next page you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll come to that in a minute. While we're still on this page we see your estimated number of terrorist losses was around 70 dead, and once again no prisoners were taken, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under item number 2 it lists the total forces engaged in these operations --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think about 820 from the -- from your sources, plus 180 from the 243rd plus about 1.020 from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S and at page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You go in some detail what happened on the first day and what happened on the second day, the third day, et cetera. And as I read these I see a couple of entries that seemed to indicate that the army did enter villages, and I thought you had told us before that your forces did not do that. When you say that, do you mean nobody from the 549th and subordinate units or do you mean nobody from the army at all entered villages and then it was only MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What villages are you talking about specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, where you're talking about the first day, second paragraph in my English says: "Forces from the 15th armoured brigade," top of page 3 in English," ... seized Malisevo," and then they "continued to breakthrough." Battle Group 5 of the 549th Detachment and the 37th PJP Detachment ... had complete seized Dobrodeljane village ... Battle Group 2 of the 243rd with some MUP from the 37th... completely seized Semetiste village..." Does that not mean that those forces were in those villages?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here what you're talking about the 15th Armoured Brigade and 243rd Brigade, those were my neighbouring units, and you can see here that the MUP and the army forces on both axes were together and that they entered those villages. If you want to continue on, you have to pass through those villages. In the village of Dobrodeljane there is one road leading through it and you cannot move towards Pagarusa any by other way, you have to take that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think in some of your earlier testimony you told us about forces going around those villages, but this one says Battle Group 5 of the 549th and the 37th completely seized the village. Are you telling us they seized the village by passing through it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that the forces didn't enter the villages. When there were MUP forces present, if there was any civilian population and if anything needed to be done, if a village needed to be -- or if the population needed to be controlled, that's what the MUP units did. But it is quite natural that the army units moved through those villages together with the MUP units, and the village of Dobrodeljane had already been abandoned by the civilians and it was completely fortified for defence. So the fighting for this village lasted several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go down to about the fourth paragraph from the bottom on your page that's on the screen, General, it talks about during the third day remaining areas were mopped up. And at the end it says: "The forces of the 5th PJP Company and parts of the 15th Armoured Brigade were joined in Belanica village, where they evacuated and cared for some 30.000 refugees." To where were these 30.000 refugees evacuated?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written here, I personal didn't reach Belanica and it wasn't on my axis. From my axis, some of the civilians went towards Belanica village. This was written by my operations officer. He must have learned it from his contacts with other units. As for the population, I believe one part went towards Suva Reka and another part went via Malisevo towards Orahovac. Those were the two routes the civilian population could take.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. In that same portion about the events on the third day, you mention the Glavica feature. What was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me exactly which paragraph that -- oh, I see. It's a feature, a hill, that was particularly well fortified and it prevented this Battle Group 5 and the 37th Detachment from advancing further towards Pagarusa village. It was a well-fortified hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Spat feature, what was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similarly, a hill surrounded by trenches from which terrorists put up strong resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. It says that: "The 23rd PJP Detachment and Battle Group 6 of the 549th reached the Glavica feature, which enabled Battle Group 5 of 549th and forces of the 37th PJP Detachment to seize the Spat feature and enter Pagarusa village, taking all streets of Pagarusa village." So isn't that an example of some of your forces entering a village? Weren't elements of the Battle Group 5 of the 549th in Pagarusa village?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were together with MUP units. This reference here means -- because we don't have the map on which this is shown, that the 37th Detachment and Battle Group 5 were unable for several days to make a step further until Battle Group 6 and another detachment arrived from another axis, from behind, and acting from the rear and from the flank they managed to force the terrorists to leave these features, and it was only then that these forces were able to enter Pagarusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, here we see your signature and your stamp. Where did this specific document come from? It does not appear to have a VJ archive stamp on it. We see no other stamp for your brigade or any delivery stamp, anything like that. Can you tell us where this one specifically came from? I understand that we got this when you testified in the Milosevic case. Did you bring it from your personal collection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is document from the Prosecution's collection and I believe from the heading that it was used in the Milosevic case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, that's exactly what Mr. Hannis has said, and he's looking for its original source and he thinks Mr. Delic may be able to assist. Please answer that, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like with any other document, the source is the archive; however, it doesn't bear the stamp of the archive. This document must have been seized much earlier, when the military archive was governed by completely different rules. I know when I was preparing for a different testimony I was given the opportunity to go to the military archive and to review for that occasion various documents, and when I chose the documents I believed to be relevant I received them without a stamp. Nowadays the situation is different. I went again recently to the military archive, and nowadays each document bears two stamps, one from the military archive and another stamp of the government's commission, I believe, for cooperation with this Tribunal. I know this for sure, it is my document, I signed it, I know what's in it, I know who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, on some of the documents that we see, some of the documents we have received have a stamp referring to the commission for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. There's no such stamp on this document. Can you tell us when there was a change in the rules of the archive. You say this must have been seized much earlier. When was there a change in process at the archives, if you know.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in 2004, and this last thing, since I went to the archive again in July and August this year and I saw certain documents that nowadays have two stamps on the front page, I was surprised because in addition to the archive stamp they have the stamp of the commission for cooperation. But I believe that is true of 2007. I don't know about 2006. The documents that I wanted, that I needed, I received in 2007, and they now have two stamps on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying before 2004 documents would be kept at the archive without having any VJ archive stamp on them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stamps do not preserve documents. I notice there are different practices. If somebody requested a document and that document was found in the archive and sent to a certain address, it certainly had a stamp. But I simply don't know. I know about the documents that I received, that they did not have a stamp. All I was required to do was to show up there and produce a permit, an approval, to choose the documents, and ask for copies. There are a certain number of documents with stamps and some without.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whatever that practice may have been and is now, are you comfortable and confident looking at this document that this is one that was prepared and signed by you on or about that date in March 1999, late March or early April 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this certainly didn't happen in the end of March, it was sometime in the first days of April, but it's certainly the document. It's my signature here, plus I remember reading this document after the operations officer drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. General, I want to move now for a while to Joint Command. You spoke quite a bit about it during your testimony in the Milosevic case. I want to try and confirm with you some of the statements you made there, and I believe you told us in connection with the Pristina Corps order number 455-115, for which we saw the envelope as an exhibit and you explained that you received it in that envelope, I guess delivered by a courier?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that envelope there was the order that said "Joint Command" on it. That was one thing that was in the envelope, right? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That envelope contained the order, a section of a map, and I believe something else related to artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you told us that --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps something else related to engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you told us that it had the order with Joint Command written on it, it had the map, the section of the map for you, and then it had one or two other documents for the engineering personnel and the artillery personnel, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe concerning engineers there was yet another map showing which roads were mined or perhaps an order for the engineers, something for artillery, something for engineers; but as for personnel, if I said it then, then there may have been an order like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I recall, did you not tell us that those documents for engineering and artillery did not have a reference to the Joint Command on them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, Mr. Hannis. Part of it was missed because of overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I went too fast. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I think you told us before that those documents for the engineering and artillery personnel did not contain a reference to Joint Command on them, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Joint Command was never written on those documents. There was command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us that it was, if not the constant practice, it was a regular occurrence that before you received a written order like this with the Joint Command on it, that you would get a verbal order or you would get a phone call from General Lazarevic that you were going to be receiving an order, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally it is my duty to talk to the commander every day; however, when the war began it was no longer possible to talk to him every day on the phone because the repeaters were destroyed and I talked to him through other communications. I talked to him as often as possible. It was the practice with General Pavkovic in 1998 and General Lazarevic in 1999, in the morning when I told them what was new in my unit and what the problems were, they would tell me that I would receive an order before the end of the day. Sometimes they would send me preparatory order by telegram so that I could prepare for a certain activity. When I received an envelope like that, I knew that some new activity was ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to 1998 and the five-stage plan for combatting terrorism, in Milosevic you told us that it was your understanding that Joint Command was intended for that plan. That was why it existed in 1998. Do you recall saying that? I'm referring to page number 41600, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe I answered his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know I spoke about the Joint Command on more than one occasion. I was asked by Mr. Nice more than once and I would really like if you have a specific question -- because somehow I don't remember saying that there was a Joint Command for this five-stage plan. I would like to see that if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to bring it up or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to now refer you to your answer, this is at page 41600, 30 June 2005. Your answer at line 15 says: "My explanation of why it says 'Joint Command' is the following: In the course of 1998, when together with members of the MUP we carried out activities against the terrorists in those five stages that I have already explained, at the beginning of each stage were invited to come to Pristina." So maybe I haven't artfully phrased my question but isn't that your understanding of what the Joint Command was for, was to help coordinate that five-stage plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said is not consistent with your question. What I said in 2005 I repeated to you yesterday in exactly the same terms and I said the very same thing again today, namely, that I went to Pristina only when my unit was involved in one of the activities of that five-stage plan, and that happened two or three times, whereas in your previous question you said something quite different. And I doubt it that I could have said in 2005 that the Joint Command had been set up for this five-stage plan. What I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go on to 41601 you're still talking about the Joint Command and you say at line 6: "And I understand this Joint Command is a coordinating body between the army and the MUP and the other state organs in Pristina." At line 10 Judge Kwon asked you: "Was there any legal or practical basis to establish this kind of Joint Command?" And at line 12 you say: "Well, as far as the fight against terrorism is concerned the state can use different mechanisms and organize all its resources after all."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here that I have just stated my opinion as to what the state should do. In response to Judge Kwon's question I could not have given an answer based on practical knowledge because I never saw a Joint Command, I never saw an order establishing a Joint Command, I never saw those people, nor did I attend a meeting of the Joint Command that would enable me to say some more about it. That was just my thinking, my reasoning in response to one of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the Joint Command in 1998, were you aware of who the participants were?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again, in my mind there is no Joint Command, it doesn't exist. In my mind, there is just the command of the Pristina Corps. Apart from my commander, his Chief of Staff was somebody sometimes from the army. I used to see people from the MUP on certain occasions as well, but nobody ever told me, These are members of the Joint Command or this here is the Joint Command. A Joint Command is just a term, a concept for me that exists for the purposes of implementing some sort of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you agree that such a body did exist. Your disagreement is about whether it had the ability to command --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either we are attending two different trials or I don't know what this is leading to. The man is saying he never heard about it, he has no clue, something like that doesn't exist; and the Prosecution responds by saying, So you agree it exists. I don't know how many times it needs to be said or maybe we are into numbers. We have to say this something 20 or 30 times. In my system it needs to be said only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got your point, Mr. Fila, just calm down and we'll deal with it. Mr. Hannis, the witness has not said that he agrees such a body exists; he says it's a concept reflecting coordination, and that's what's given rise to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'll refer you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to either rephrase that or find some foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 41602 you say at line 2: "I actually never saw this Joint Command, I never attended a single meeting, I only came across individual persons, if I can put it that way, and I had heard of some persons being in Pristina. At any rate, I was supposed to be in Pristina and I could go to Pristina only when told to do so by the command." Line 7: "I know that in this coordination body Mr. Minic was there for a while and Mr. Sainovic and then I think Mr. Matkovic as far as the civilian authorities are concerned. I don't know whether it was Mr. Andjelkovic too. As for MUP now, was it Mr. Djordjevic. As far as the army was concerned, it was probably the corps commander." So are those the individuals you understood to be involved in this, what you call, a coordinating body that coordinated the activities of the MUP and VJ in carrying out joint operations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on that occasion I said something that is quite different from this, and you'll probably find it in the text. Concerning those people, I heard they were there. I heard from local self government that they were in charge of civil affairs. They were primarily in Pristina as representatives of the government in order to contact with international representatives who were numerous in Pristina, in order to be able to contact with humanitarian organizations and local self governments in Kosovo and Metohija. And I believe that was their primary task. And I said the same thing then, but I don't know which examination it was because even back then Mr. Nice asked me a dozen of times over some 10 or 20 days about a Joint Command, and I said even then the Joint Command is just a concept, it doesn't exist, because if it existed it had to be embodied by certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, one other thing you said about that was at page 42032 [Realtime transcript read in error "42072"], 7th of July, you're again talking about the Joint Command, saying: "I didn't pay any attention to this term 'Joint Command' because I usually received on a regular basis orders from my superior command at the Pristina Corps. Of course this was on TV every day that a group of politicians, state officials from the republican and federal governments was in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that in Pristina there was a staff of the MUP for combatting terrorism, there was the command of the Pristina Corps as well, there was certainly meetings taking place between the two, but as for this group of politicians they were primarily to monitor the development of the political and security situation of Kosovo and Metohija." And at line 21: "To coordinate with the MUP and the army." So whether I call them the Joint Command or you call them the coordinating body, there was a mixed group of politicians, VJ, and MUP that were coordinating those actions, those military combat actions, being carried out jointly by the MUP and the VJ in 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. As for coordination between MUP and the army, it probably existed, because on the orders of my commander I implemented that coordination on my lower level as well. As for other civilian structures, I have already explained what kind of affairs they were -- that they could have been engaged in Kosovo and Metohija, and I said they were representatives of the government because of the problems that prevailed in Kosovo and Metohija, because of local self governments and all the other things that the government had to take care of in Kosovo and Metohija, certainly not because of police or military actions, because that would be completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeated for the umpteenth time, what Mr. Hannis just read does not contain the word "body" and on page 42072 there is no reference to that. Can I beg you, please show me first on the screen what Mr. Hannis is reading and then we can read it together in the same way and then ask the witness, because this is the second time already that one thing is being read and another thing is written or it's not even there. Let us be all on the same page, literally, otherwise it's not a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dealing with the question that was posed first of all, the question Mr. Hannis posed is justified on the basis of what he quoted and the witness has answered the question, dealt with it. What Mr. Hannis says is not evidence is what the witness says, and he's testing him quite properly in this question on his previous evidence and what he said in this trial. So far as showing us the pages you're referring to, Mr. Hannis, would you care to do that or is it going to cause a particular problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't recall that I was reading from the page that is in the transcript cited by Mr. Fila, 42072 was not the page I was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 41602 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did read from 41602 and I think I read from 42032, not 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's quoted in the transcript as 42072 in line 19 on page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, can we have the right page on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I determine which one we're referring to now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you say 42032, although you're recorded as saying 72. If you're finished with it, of course it's the next one we want to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't want to see 42032?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Fila's point is an ongoing point that it facilitates the exercise if the pages are on the screen, but since you've completed that one, we can do that with the subsequent ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, thank you. The next one I want to read from is 42128.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you recall telling the Court during the Milosevic trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a question over what -- are these exhibits in the trial or are they simply going to be retrieved from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this transcript has a 3 or 4D number, but we're checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Various shaking of heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may check on that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may not be uploaded into e-court. I know it was on our notification to the Defence that it was something that we would use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't announce it, the fact that Mr. Hannis mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding what you've said. In English it's translated as: "We didn't announce it, the fact that Mr. Hannis mentioned it."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I -- with your leave, Your Honour. I heard from Mr. Hannis that he mentioned it some -- the Defence announced that exhibit, but just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, he said he gave notice to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have to check that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm checking, Your Honour. I think I have a 3D reference. On our notification we indicated that we would use the transcript of the testimony of General Delic from the Milosevic trial, and we made a reference to Exhibit Number 3D00524, which is in e-court apparently and it's a total of 2.230 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the whole evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's his entire testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That should be your source when you wish to ask another question based on his previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecution counsel is kindly requested to switch off the short microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- do you recall testifying about a body. Body called the inter-departmental staff that you said existed before the Joint Command. I'm referring to page 42128 in that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I just have in front of me the hard copy of the letter from OTP, and the first number is 3D580 and there is no -- oh, yeah, okay. That makes sense. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'd like to see it up on the screen that I mentioned the Joint Command, where was that. Certainly there was some knowledge on my part that in the MUP there was some inter-departmental staff from an earlier period, but I don't have any deeper knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying about when the fifth stage of the plan for combatting terrorism began. My note indicates you said that started on the 25th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I might have said that, that it was in September 1998, because I think that at that time that was when the last phase of the plan took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you recall that the OSCE and KVM verifiers arrived on the scene in Kosovo sometime after that five-stage plan was completed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The verifiers arrived at the end of October, and the plan was completed quite a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. With regard to the verifiers, we have heard some evidence or seen some evidence that on at least one occasion, if not more, when the KVM attempted to enter the border zone and tried to move a barricade to do so a soldier on duty was to cock his weapon and give a warning to tell the KVM to stay out. Is that an order that you issued?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly wasn't an order that I issued; however, it is certainly a violation of the agreement by the verifiers because in the border belt you could enter the border belt only accompanied by a liaison officer, whereas in all other areas you could go to them without any restrictions. And can you imagine what the situation would have been like if somebody were to enter the border belt and lift the ramp himself. It's like somebody opening your front door without asking you. That is impermissible behaviour on the part of the verifiers. I am not justifying the soldiers in my unit, that is perhaps one case that we investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you hadn't issued an order like that and a soldier had done that, was he doing that on his own or an order from somebody else regarding a standing procedure on the border belt?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier was acting exclusively according to standard procedure and the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who had established that procedure, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That procedure is provided for in the rules and relates to the guards service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you had some volunteers in the 549th, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1999, after the beginning of the war, there were volunteers too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many volunteers were in the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a lot. If you count those who were on the territory -- well, there might have been at all events several hundred I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a unit or group called the Ibar Wolves, I-b-a-r Wolves?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, I've never heard of a unit like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you heard of a TV journalist named Milovan Drecun, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know that journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to conclude that this question by Mr. Hannis will lead to a photograph taken from Milovan Drecun's book and which was announced after the witness took the solemn declaration and began his testimony, and the explanation I was given with respect to Wesley Clark's book and parts of that book - and I think that the same standards should be applied and indeed for other books when we don't have the author testifying before this Trial Chamber the same rules should apply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is your objection? Is it to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That kind of evidence cannot be used, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to my understanding the objection is that I was late in notifying the intent to use this, and that's true, I was; but I do notify him on Thursday or Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he then went on to explain that he's really basing this on a decision we made about the use of Wesley Clark's book because he was not going to be here as a witness, but you'll remember that that was connected to the fact that his presence here had been opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah -- yes, Your Honour. What I'm proposing to do is to show the General a photograph from that book that purports to be a group of volunteers for the 549th and just ask him if he recognises any of those individuals or is aware of the existence of that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. For that exercise it wouldn't matter where the photograph came from, so please proceed with the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If we could -- if I could find the exhibit number first, Your Honour, that would help. I know it's in the 3.000 series, but I don't have the page. I wonder if we might take the break a minute early while I collect myself and find that book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Lunchtime come early, Mr. Delic. Can you please leave the courtroom as usual, and we'll see you in an hour's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The court will resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan will not be sitting with us this afternoon for urgent personal reasons. We've decided it's in the interests of justice that we should continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when we broke I started to ask you about volunteers, but I realized there's one last thing I need to do in regard to our discussion about Joint Command. I want to show you an exhibit, document P2166 -- and actually I've got a hard copy here if the usher would hand it to you. It's multiple pages. It might be easier. These are the minutes of a meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I don't know whether this witness is able to give us reliable information about a meeting he did not attend, and this is a record of a meeting of the inter-departmental staff from 1998. It was attended by various persons but not by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's wait and see what the question is first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, my first question is: Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps during his examination Mr. Milosevic showed me this or a similar document, asking him -- asking me on that occasion to tell him who attended from the army and who attended from the police. It could be this one, it could be a similar one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you finish what you started to say? It looks like you got cut off.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic -- I believe he asked me about the lines of -- the chains of command. He asked me whether at any time in 1998 or 1999 the chain of command in the army was disrupted. I said no, and then he produced a document like this for me to read but only the part that specifies who attended. He asked me whether the Chief of the General Staff attended, I said yes; whether the commander of the 3rd Army was present, I said yes; whether the commander of the Pristina Corps attended, I said yes. And then he said, Is this beginning with me until the Pristina Corps level the complete chain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's stop. This is not anything to do with what we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, let's control these answers which Mr. Delic, no doubt is giving with the best will in the world but really don't assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you see who the attendees are and they include your superiors in the army, as well as high-ranking police and political officials. In the second paragraph you see that Mr. Milosevic is telling this operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism about what's going to happen at the meeting and he indicates that General Pavkovic is going to present the proposals of the Joint Command. Given who's attending and what's described here, does that change your mind about whether or not a body called the Joint Command existed in 1998. It's being discussed at the highest levels. You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not affect me in the least --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I have already said what I thought about the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can stop there. The next paragraph General Pavkovic gives a brief report on the implementation of the plan for suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and says, speaking on behalf of the Joint Command, General Pavkovic reminded the members of the operations staff that the plan had been carried out in five stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we'll need to go to the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He said the plan had been carried out in five stages with a duration of 45 to 55 days, commencing on 25 July, completed on 29 October 1998. Is that consistent with your experience and what you knew about the five-stage plan? You told us there was a five-stage plan and you were involved in some of those actions pursuant to the plan. Is that accurate, five stages, 45 to 55 days, July to October?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my unit, it completed its activities earlier. The 29th of October is mentioned here, but my unit completed all its activities in the beginning of October. At that time I had heard of the five-stage plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you and your units had engaged in actions pursuant to that plan, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We participated pursuant to orders we received from our superior command, that is, the Pristina Corps. My commanding officers had no idea that this was part of a five-stage plan. They received my orders and executed them, whereas I had heard talk of a five-stage plan for combatting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And at page 3, going on to page 4 of the B/C/S, and it's page 3 of the English, General Pavkovic is talking about the task set out in the said plan. I want to go to page 4 of both the English and B/C/S. Item number 4 is: "Arming the Serbian and Montenegrin people and establishing reserve police units to defend Serbian villages." Did you or your units take any part in that task under the plan? Did you have anything to do with arming the Serbian and Montenegrin people?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of that happened in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about number 7: "Disarming all Siptar villages which are known to be armed," did you and your troops not assist in that in your area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit participated in that task too, but the disarming of Siptar villages did not involve combat. In carrying out this task, there were no combat operations. We talked to the seniors of villages, whereas some villages, even before we reached them, had sent out their representatives and the arms that they had previously received from terrorists. They brought on tractors and trucks to our unit saying they did not need them. So I participated in this seventh task in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there are documents related.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears it's still General Pavkovic talking about -- and here he's talking about some of the detailed information in implementing the plan. The fifth item says: "Since 29 July 1998, operations were conducted in 306 populated places, including ..." And you'll see further on it says "47 in Prizren ..." And that "the operations encompassed 19 municipalities in four towns," including Orahovac. Is that consistent with what you saw and what you were doing on the ground, operations during this five-phase plan were carried out in 47 populated places in Prizren? I assume that means Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done by General Pavkovic. He is the best-placed to answer. I didn't count, but a number of settlements including Orahovac and other places within the border belt where these activities were carried out, I don't know whether that would be 47 settlements. But if it's written here, I believe it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your subordinate units would have been involved in a significant number of those, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units subordinated to me participated only in activities ordered by the superior command, otherwise they were involved in in-depth security of the state border; and I'm not sure whether this covers incidents that occurred during incursions by terrorist groups that smuggled weapons into our countries because such incidents were very frequent in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I take this to mean that there were anti-terrorist operations, joint operations, with the MUP carried out in 47 populated places in Prizren municipality. Are you telling us that your units didn't participate in all or a significant number of those? Who else would have done it if not your guys?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that my units did not take part, but I cannot state now that it was 47 places. I assume that since General Pavkovic wrote that, that it's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in compiling this information, a report to Mr. Milosevic and the other big-shots on his committee, wouldn't he have gotten information from you about what happened in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somehow -- I don't know. But did you use this word "zverka" big-shot, which is not appropriate if you're talking about state leaders. It was translated by the word "zverka." I would rather put it politicians of high level or high-level policemen, because when you say "zverka," or beast in literal translation, big-shot, it means something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Please now answer the question, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent information to Mr. Pavkovic, and that information or those documents probably exist because they were used in the Milosevic trial, and I think that the number, 47, is perhaps a little excessive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume there were 47 in Prizren municipality. Can we also assume that you would be involved in all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything that happened in the Prizren municipality I certainly took part in, because the Prizren municipality has maybe over a hundred or 150 settlements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to page 6 of the B/C/S, stay on 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Pavkovic also reports that large quantities of ammunition were confiscated and he says at the top of your page 6: "93 Siptar villages were disarmed," including 38 in Prizren. You -- is that consistent with your memory and your experience during this five-stage plan? Do you have any reason to disagree with that number of 38 villages being disarmed in Prizren municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "Prizren municipality," I cannot agree with that, but I would agree if it was said in the Prizren district, for example, because the Prizren district comprises several municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that would make it correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I'll accept that. Thank you. Let me see if there was one more question I had for you from this document. No, General, let me move on to something else. Regarding that five-phase plan we have a document in evidence Exhibit P1468, which purports to be notes of meetings of the Joint Command in 1998, and it talks about some of the phases of the plan to combat terrorism. At page 30 and 33 of the English regarding the 30th of July, 1998, there is a meeting about initiating the third phase of the plan. Do you recall participating in the third phase of the five-stage plan in late July or early August 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to know what that third phase was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And likewise, there's a reference in those minutes [sic] to the fourth stage being planned in early August, around the 4th and 5th of August, being realized on the 8th and continued on the 12th of August. Do you recall being involved in the fourth phase?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again I'd like to ask that attention be paid to the words being used. The Prosecutor said that these were minutes from the meeting of the Joint Command, minutes I think he called them, whereas you don't have the minutes nor do the minutes exist, but he is persisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I said "notes."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try and look at the notes of a number of authors because there are at least two documents which are handwritten and they're certainly not minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis has already tried to indicate there that he withdraws that reference and will continue to call them notes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did say notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you said "minutes" according to the question, line 7, page 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I said notes there, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, do you recall having participated in the fourth stage of the plan to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you have to tell me what that fourth phase was for me to be able to say whether I took part or not. I have just got something up on my screen now but I am looking at it for the first time and it doesn't really mean anything. So if there's anything there you want me to read through, I'll need a little time to do that; but as far as I can see this is just an ordinary piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't have time to go through that with you. Let me move on to what I started to ask you about before we broke, and I'd like to show you Exhibit 3047. Do you recognise that page that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This looks like a book, because it says Milovan Drecun, "The Second Battle of Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you not seen or read that book yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the book, but it looks a little different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that at or around the time that book was published or released, General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic went and spoke at that event?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just base for the previous question, I'm just wondering about it. This is the first time I hear that information related to that book and the presence of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was only a question and the answer was no. But, Mr. Hannis, what's the -- I don't know why there's anxiety because it's not evidence in the case as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question is based on information I have from an interview and from internal leadership research team documents provided to me. I can provide that to Mr. Cepic if I'm required to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you should, not at this minute, but you should give him the information if it hasn't already been disclosed to him. I imagine it has but you can locate it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you see this picture and the caption says: "Heroes of the defence of Gorozup: The volunteers of the 549th Motorised Brigade." Have you seen this picture before? Have you seen this photograph before, before today?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how is it that you're familiar with the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in Leskovac on the 16th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how do you know that? Were you there at the time or somebody tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my brigade on the 14th and on the 14th of June with the last soldiers of my brigade I received Leskovac. This is the south camp barracks there; that was where my brigade was to be put up. And this is -- this photograph was taken in front of the kitchen area of that unit. These are the volunteers that were giving back their equipment and uniforms because they were being released from the unit that day. Those in civilian clothing were going straight home, the others were going to give back their weapons. So they invited me, since the 16th of June is Army Day, to be in the photograph with them before they dispersed and left the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that you on the steps in the upper right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You look like the third face down if I start from the upper right, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Gorozup, what does that refer to? Is that a geographic location? Is that a border post?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gorozup is a border hut on the border with Albania, border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what do you know about how this group got to be called heroes of the defence of Gorozup? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the writer of the book. The author of the book wanted to acknowledge them especially because the border post was destroyed during the NATO bombing, and after when the attack from Albania came it was taken control of. And the following day, because you can see that there's some border soldiers here, and this group of people, probably some are missing here, but anyway this group of people managed to regain control of that border post, whereas in the BBC, CNN, and other newspaper agencies Jamie Shea said that the border had been broken through -- perhaps he didn't mention this particular border post, but anyway he said that the terrorist forces have reached the valley of Drina and were at the entrance to Prizren. Milan Drecun came to this border post and met these people here, and then he sent out a photograph that same evening out to the world about the lies told by NATO and he said the border post in Gorozup has not fallen --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. When was this group of volunteers activated? When did they become a part of the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they came in at different times, but anyway in April, in April, in May, and they even came in at the beginning of June as well as they were sent from the collection centres in Belgrade and in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were they dispersed among your various units? Were they all in one unit or were they divided up among all your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the units, there were volunteers in all the units depending on what their speciality was. Those who were infantry men were in the infantry units, the artillery men were in the artillery units, and so on; and those who were, for example, quartermasters, signalsmen, and so on, they were in those kind of units, the kind of unit they were members of when they did their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Russians, did you have any Russian volunteers in the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere towards the end of April I received the first group -- well, they weren't only Russians. There were others there too, but there were Russians too, Russians, Ukrainians and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there not a group of Russians and/or Ukrainians that was taken in as an entity, as a compact group into the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by taken as an entity, as a compact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That they were not subordinated to one of your main group but they formed a unique unit unto themselves?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. The Russians who came and all those who came later were within one unit, in order to enable mutual communication, but there weren't any Russians in that group. There were Russians, Ukrainians, Serbs, one Macedonian, a Bulgarian. But the Russians were the most numerous of the foreigners, if I can put it that way, and they didn't go to other units because then there would be the problem of communication. That's why they were all put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the name or the numerical designator for that group of Russian, Ukrainian, and other volunteers? What did you call them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have any special name. They were just a platoon and there was a total of about 30 of them, half of them were foreigners and the other half were soldiers and military recruits, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that they were involved in actions in April 1999, how would you refer to that? If you were writing an order, how would you refer to that group? You must have had some name or term to refer to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were the intervention platoon, and that's what they were known under.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the only intervention platoon in the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which part of your brigade was involved in retaking the border hut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people on the picture here. I can't say exactly which of them took part, but since the photograph was provided by one of the volunteers, given to Mr. Drecun, then some of these people did take part in that. What I know is that the border platoon took part from the Gorozup border post, and that one platoon from my own unit took part, and that was composed of both soldiers and of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when we're looking at this group who are described as volunteers, we're not looking at an entire unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not a whole unit because the border battalion, the 55th, defending that part of the state border was redeployed to Leskovac in another place at that time. And I don't think, or rather, I don't think it was in Leskovac at all, I think it was in Vranje or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The group we see, though, these are all volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know why they would be described as "the volunteers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are ordinary soldiers there too in that group, but most of them were volunteers. And as you can see, on that day they returned -- they were about to return their uniforms and the weapons they had been issued in order to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this whole group were fighting together in one -- they were involved in combat together in one unit, were they, one part of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group that we can see here on the photograph, they're different volunteers, probably from different units, and amongst them there were those who did indeed fight at Gorozup. And I remember them wanting to be photographed with me before their departure. So that I can't say that all of them were volunteers who were at Gorozup, but all the people in the photograph were in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You really can't tell us how many of these men there were volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see on this photograph, perhaps four to five were soldiers and all the rest were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, military recruits and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell us if all of them were involved in the assault on the border hut at Gorozup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm certain that not all of them took part. Some of them did, but I can't know which of those in the picture did defend the Gorozup border post and later on took control of it, or rather, liberated it from the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just no idea how many of them fall into that category, roughly even?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't know that for certain. They were there in order to return their weapons and uniforms, everything they'd been issued. I happened to pass by at the time and some of them asked me to come and join them in the photograph so that they would have a keepsake because they were supposed to leave the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you aware whether anyone has challenged the book as being an inaccurate account of the event or showing an inaccurate photograph related to the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't see any need to challenge this photograph or to challenge the book in any way.
