What you see here are people who for the most part were volunteers in my brigade. Now, whether they were at Gorozup or whether they fought in some other place is not essential. They all took part in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I would like to show you right now Exhibit P1479 concerning volunteers. Were you aware of a Supreme Command Staff order forbidding volunteer units, and we can see this is from the 7th of April, 1999. We have to actually go to the next page, I think it's item 8, so I'm not sure if that's page 2 or 3 of both the English and the B/C/S. Yeah, it's -- item 8 says: "When assigning volunteers to VJ commands and installations, it is prohibited to group them within one unit, task, or the like, given earlier negative experiences with a number of volunteers looting, setting fire to houses, et cetera." Were you not aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very well-acquainted with this order and I acted upon it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you do anything to disband the intervention platoon made up of those Russian and Ukrainian volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Russian and Ukrainian volunteers were together with the military recruits and other volunteers and soldiers from my brigade. They were volunteers only by token of the fact that they had come of their own free will to fight in our country. They weren't any special type of volunteer unit, and I did not have a single volunteer unit myself. All I had was volunteers deployed in the various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I misunderstood your earlier answer. Who were members of this intervention platoon other than those Russians, Ukrainians, one Macedonian, and a Serb I think? Weren't they all volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all of them were volunteers. Among them there were military recruits and there was a number of soldiers from the reconnaissance unit and the military police company to the level of a squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of that platoon, well there was one komandir, commander, was a Serb, and the other commander was a Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that Russian named Dimjan Balan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Russian's name was Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was a captain at one time in the Russian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a couple of other photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I assume - and I hope my assumption is correct - that my colleague Mr. Hannis will be using a set of photographs and a statement by the man Dimjan mentioned a moment ago. The statement was given to the investigators of the Tribunal in June 2006, so far before this trial started. So we have an objection of principle that such documents cannot be used, and among others we should have been supplied the material under disclosure pursuant to Rule 66 or 68, depending on the contents of the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just one more remark. We received the material a few hours before this witness took the solemn declaration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I state that such documents should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not being allowed. What is it you're actually objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood it that Mr. Hannis, the Prosecutor, wishes to use those documents now, Your Honour; that's what he was going to do now, that he was going to use some of those documents, the documents that I'm objecting to, before he begins showing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your objection as I read it is in relation to this person called Dimjan -- I've lost the name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Balan, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Balan. Are you going to be asking more questions about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking about some photographs and documents. I'm not going to be asking about his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is it you say -- I'm sorry, Mr. Cepic, I'm just not following this. You'll need to spell it out to me in words of one syllable that I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for confusion which I made, I will try to explain this as simply as I can. This material, statement and in addition to that statement a couple of photographs, we received same day when Mr. Delic started to testify before this Honourable Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand this material Prosecutor has got in the previous time probably from 3rd of June, 2006, and I think that they had to disclose to us in a previous period, not on the same day when the witness started to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was not a witness we called, he was not on our 65 ter list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cepic is saying this is material that should have been disclosed a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that there was any Rule 68 in it, and Rule 66 did not apply since he was not going to be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Cepic. On what basis do you say that this should have been disclosed at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to my humble opinion Rule 66 or 68. Unfortunately, I was involved in this case after this period, but I think that there were some obligation for disclosure of material in the previous period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is that in this Tribunal, and indeed in many other places, there's no obligation on the Defence to disclose their witnesses until after the Prosecution case is over. And in this instance it appears the individual involved was not envisaged as a Prosecution witness, Mr. Delic is not a Prosecution witness, the matter arises in the presentation of the Defence case. There is, on the face of it, no reason why this material should have been disclosed at any earlier stage, other than the point at which it was decided if it should be used for the purposes of cross-examination. So therefore we will allow Mr. Hannis to make use of these two photographs. If it comes to the statement, which he's indicated he's not using, we will review the position again in relation to the statement. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, first I'd like to show you Exhibit P3045. This is a photograph. And can you tell us who's depicted there. That's you in the middle in uniform, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know those other two standing beside you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two of the Russian volunteers who remained in Serbia. They lived in Serbia after the conflict. One of them is Dimjan or Dima that you mentioned and the other one with the eye-patch is Albert. They stayed in Serbia after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it correct that this photograph was taken about a year after the war upon the occasion of your promotion and Brigade Day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This photograph was taken on the 17th of July, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the occasion that you all happened to be at the same place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of July is the day of the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look next at Exhibit P3039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to wonder about how that previous exchange was interpreted. Were you promoted on that day, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was promoted on the 31st of December, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That explains it. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I would like to show you Exhibit P3039. I don't know if you can see that well enough on your screen. I have an enlargement in hard copy with just the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If there's no objection I would hand that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, this calls for an objection because we really don't know. This is a handwritten. There is something below the actual picture which is handwritten. I see that it has translated, and we can -- we cannot possibly really find out who wrote it, when it was written, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same objection, but this definitely could not have been written by the witness giving the statement. There is a sample of his handwriting in that statement and that is not -- that is definitely not the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well these objections are premature. We do not know what the question is yet, and the question may have nothing to do with the writing. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, from that photo can you recognise that the person sitting on the far right on the front row is Dimjan Balan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You can see that it's him there on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on the uniforms, can you tell us who this group of people is or what organization they may belong to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say that because this photograph is fairly dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these are members of the army, whether there are any army personnel here, or whether these are policemen. This photograph is rather unclear and it is impossible to discern the colours of the uniforms, but you can see here on the right side, in the right flank, you can see this Russian volunteer, Dima.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was a member of the VJ, he was not a member of the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that help you to identify who these people might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Now this is even worse, this photograph. You can't even recognise him on this photograph as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the hard copy you have, could you look at the third individual from the left on the second row. Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very unclear. If you have an indication as to who that might be, you perhaps may tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have an indication that that's Radislav Mitrovic from the 37th PJP Detachment. You knew him, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Colonel, or rather, Lieutenant-Colonel Mitrovic, as he was at that time, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this photograph is really very bad quality and I can't really claim that it is him, although it does look like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. General, do you wear contact lenses or glasses?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use glasses to watch TV and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During 1999 did you wear glasses?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that year too, but only, as I already said, to drive and to watch TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I next want to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move, does that version on the screen help you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a bit better. It is obvious now that these are police members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that any better or worse than the picture of the third individual on the left from the second row?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see that better too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that help you say whether or not it's Lieutenant-Colonel Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be Lieutenant-Colonel Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you Exhibit 3042, P3042. This purports to be a certificate indicating that Dimjan Balan, a volunteer, was within the formation of the 549th between the 2nd of April and the 13th of June, 1999. It has your name, but it doesn't appear to be -- well, I can't tell if there's a signature or a stamp or not. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, because there's no stamp of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's dated the 8th of January, 2000. Do you recall issuing such a document for Mr. Balan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the fighting --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my humble opinion this was material that was subject to Rule 68 and that we were supposed to get this document that is in front of us on the screen before this time, and the same goes for the photograph, some of the photographs that we have now seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what way would this be Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this pertains to the fighting in the border area in the critical period, fighting with the Siptar terrorists, and it also pertains, as far as we have been able to see, to the fighting at the very state border. And this was -- this is something that is alleged in the indictment and it is relevant for the time-period indicated in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do not see this as Rule 68 material in respect of Mr. Lazarevic, and therefore we'll allow the question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you recall my question or had I asked it yet?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you asked me the question. I don't see the stamp. A certificate should bear a stamp, and there's a number there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a request made by a volunteer who had confiscated a pistol in the fighting at the border to be allowed to keep this pistol as a trophy. But now whether it was Dimjan Balan or some other volunteer, this I can't recall at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at the next exhibit, P3040 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we do that, Your Honours, if you allow me, can I just dwell on the previous document. We object to its admission because it has not been authenticated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is 3042?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What better way might there be of checking the authenticity of a document than asking the person who appears, on the face of it, to be the author of the document, whether he is or not? Now, the witness has said he's got nothing to contribute in relation to this document; end of story. It will -- but we need it as part of the process to understand why the question was asked and how we came to be in this position. There's nothing here that counts as evidence against you. We're not going to look at the document which the witness says he can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, next I want to look at P03040. This one is dated the 30th of December, 1999, and it's described as the evaluation and opinion on the work of Dimjan Balan, a volunteer from the period of 7 April to 16 June 1999. Now, this has a stamp and your typewritten name, but that doesn't look like your signature. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see down here looks like the signature of my Chief of Staff, but I can't be certain about it, and I can't say that it was his signature but it looks like his signature as far as I am able to see. Since this document bears a number, it is possible to check whether there is a copy of this document in the unit. And I can see here that it says that this volunteer was in the unit in a certain time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and it indicates in the text that he was in the front ranks, that he was in the area of the Kosare border post and later in the area of Planeja at the beginning of the war operations, village of Budakovo. In the upper left we have a stamp that says -- I'm sorry, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of the operations. This is not true. I said that I received the first Russian volunteers on the 23rd of April, the second group I got on the 1st of June, so the 23rd of April is not the beginning of the war. That would be more towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, General, I was reading from this document that said: "In the beginning of the war operations, that is, before coming to the unit, he was in the area of Kosare Border Post and later in the area of Planeja ..." You said just now that this volunteer unit came to you on the 23rd of April and you said you said that before. I don't recall you having indicated that precise date. How is it that you remember now that it was the 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I remembered when the first group of volunteers arrived. He was in the first group. The first group arrived on the 23rd from the Kosare sector until the 23rd, so between the 2nd and the 23rd, he was not in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before he came into your unit then, when he was on the Kosare border post, in whose unit was he, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what unit he was while he was there, but the Kosare sector was defended by the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were not elements of the 72nd Special Brigade also engaged there at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elements of the 72nd Special Brigade are not part of that unit. They were in various locations carrying out tasks. In most cases they were gathering information about terrorists on the very border, and as far as I can remember it is possible that some elements of the 72nd were there indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing, Mr. Hannis, the original answer given by Mr. Delic was that the first of these volunteers arrived towards the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner we see a stamp that's translated as "military post number 4445 internal number," and there's some question mark about what that number is. Is that not a stamp of the 549th? Doesn't that pertain to your brigade.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military police 4445, that is the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, based on those stamps and what you say could be the signature of your immediate subordinate, do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the objective of this question. I was not present when this document was issued. It is just an ordinary certificate indicating that this volunteer was in the army, and if it was signed by my Chief of Staff he probably issued that for the time-period between the time when he reported to the Army of Yugoslavia and the 16th of June when he was discharged from our unit for all intents and purposes. But I do know that he was in the first group. I know that because there were four of them in that group who spoke Serbian to some extent, and I know that they came to my unit on the 23rd. As far as my unit was concerned, they were involved in combat only twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General. I want to ask you now about some of the punishment of soldiers in your unit regarding crimes that were committed within your brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P962, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you'll recognise this document I believe. This is a list of filed criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th between May 1998 and July 1999. Did you personally compile this information?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I requested that this document be drafted in my brigade. I don't know whether it was signed at all, whether there is any signature affixed to it, because several people took part in actually putting it together. The data needed to be collected from the military court in Nis too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see in the upper right-hand corner there is a signature after something that's been translated as "edited by." Do you see that and can you recognise that signature as anybody that you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "processed by," but this doesn't really mean anything to me because you can't really see that all that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, is it your understanding that this document is supposed to show all those personnel from the 549th Motorised Brigade who were subject to criminal proceedings for actions between the May 1998 and July 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not include those members against whom criminal reports were written, but the military prosecutor decided to drop the report and it doesn't include those soldiers who committed some kind of an infraction of military discipline which was less serious and which could be dealt with in the unit itself rather than a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Does it show -- well, I see there are 132 separate entries here, and if you'll trust my math, General, I would tell you that of those 132 it seems that 73 involve charges for theft of some sort, either theft, aggravated theft, vehicle theft, or receiving stolen property. So well over half regard theft, correct? Would you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think in one of your earlier answers on direct you were asked about the events on the 25th, 26th of March when we were talking about your units moving in the area of Bela Crkva and Celina, et cetera. And you were asked about allegations made by at least one of the witnesses here that looting had taken place, and you said you had only professional soldiers in your unit and professional soldiers do not loot. Isn't that correct? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. It had to do with issues related to activities from the 25th until the 28th of March, 1999, and it referred to specific places. With regard to all the soldiers in this case, it is known exactly where they committed a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I will agree with you that a number of these 73 charged with theft involve privates in the army and, I think, in some cases they may be listed -- well, I thought there were a couple that were listed as conscripts but they all seem to be mentioned as privates. The majority of those are privates, but there are at least six officers charged with some sort of theft, including a lieutenant-colonel and a major. So do you still stand by your position that professional soldiers wouldn't loot? That was a big problem in the Yugoslav Army at that time, wasn't it? We saw a lot of orders urging subordinates to pressure perpetrators of looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, is misrepresenting slightly what the witness said. When I examined in chief, we were talking about regular soldiers who were engaged in the execution of that action, not professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying that the evidence was from Mr. Delic that regular soldiers don't loot?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite, Your Honour. I asked, Who participated in this action, were they reserve soldiers or regular soldiers? The General answered, They were regular soldiers. Then I put to him the allegations by several specific witnesses regarding Celina. The witness explained that they want to steal but they have nothing to put the things they steal because they only have a rucksack on their backs with a certain kit in it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that the impression wasn't given in his evidence that an officer in his brigade would not loot, which is what Mr. Hannis is dealing with, officers, he's gone up a level?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness's words were understood differently. The General allowed for that possibility and -- in his answer and we went through several documents identifying certain officers as well in a number of thefts, looting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's said you're misrepresenting this evidence, so we'll need a reference for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm checking on that, Your Honour, and while I am may I ask another question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I recall that you did say something along the lines of what Mr. Cepic mentioned now about that they couldn't loot because they just had these little nap sacks and what could they carry with them. I ask you, sir, how big or how heavy is a role of Deutschemarks, a gold necklace, a diamond ring? Those are all things a soldier could find room for in his pocket or a nap sacks or his underwear for that matter, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely not right because you are linking what is written in that document with combat activities. In combat action, that did not happen because soldiers had their commanding soldiers with them, and that is consistent with what Mr. Cepic said and that's the way I answered him because he was asking me about the area of Celina and some Prosecution witnesses who spoke about theft and looting. The people who are on that list committed a criminal offence in some other time, not in combat action, and the injured parties were usually people who were leaving the territory of our country via the Prizren-Zur-Vrbnica road, the most -- the greatest number of crimes happened there; among them there were soldiers and commanding officers as well. I believe I did well to take all those who took -- who did such things to face a wartime court, and it doesn't matter to me what you are saying. If it was one soldier and one commanding officer, it's only -- it would be the same to me. If there had been 500, I would have taken all the 500 to the military court, and that was not a very common occurrence in my unit. If I had 14.000 men under me, 17 [as interpreted] soldiers is not even one in a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I recall that you did say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree that there's no logic in the last part of that answer, but was there something else you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: At least that last error in transcript, line 12, he said 70, 7-0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's obviously a mistake there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. To get back to the original question, Your Honour, on the 29th of November in the transcript which is numbered only pages 1 through 100 that day. At page 12, line 15, the answer was: "Only active-duty soldiers participated in this activity because there were no members who had been mobilised. Active-duty soldiers do not loot."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, if that's what you said instead of "professional," does that change your answer? I say to you, General, active-duty reserve, professional, non-professional, all kinds of soldiers loot because soldiers are human beings and some human beings loot. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put all types of soldiers in the same basket and confuse them all. I was speaking about a specific location and a specific activity, and I said that on that day, on that occasion, my soldiers were only doing their job. They were engaged in combat activity together with their commanding officers, and I assert that on that day they were not involved in any prohibited activity. This overview is backed by criminal reports from which we can see when and where these perpetrators committed the offence of robbery, theft, or any other offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, one of the reasons you said that that couldn't have happened was because they didn't have room to carry anything. We've discussed that. Another reason you said is because their commanding officers were with them, so that's another reason it could not have happened. How many soldiers did you have participating in this action in that area? How many men are we talking about, a couple hundred or more?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many commanding officers were engaged with them on that date in that area? What was the ratio? One officer for 10 men, for 20?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several dozen commanding officers from squad commanders, platoon commanders, company commanders, and battalion commanders, up to me, as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that one commanding officer could not possibly be able to keep an eye on all of the men under him during an action of this kind? Could not watch 10 or 12 men, however many he was responsible for, at every moment. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People don't need to be supervised. Most of them were brought up not to steal and not to commit criminal offences because it would be very wrong if everyone had to be watched all the time in order to prevent them -- to prevent them from committing crimes. The Rules of Service bind soldiers to honour regulations and prevent -- and it prohibits commission of crimes. Those who still did so in my unit were punished, regardless of who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, you don't allow for the possibility that one of those commanders may have engaged in looting, a commander who perhaps wasn't brought up right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All who are not brought up right are in that overview. You will see that there are some commanding officers there against whom I filed criminal reports, but it was a different time and different activities were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One thing you mentioned in an earlier answer was that you could tell -- I guess that you could tell by looking at this chart or this list you could tell when and where a crime had been committed. I see on page 1, which is -- or actually, it's page 2, the first page after the cover sheet, that there is a heading for place and time of crime, but for the overwhelming majority of entries it seems that the only thing we have is a location and most all of them seem to be either Prizren or Djakovica, with a few exceptions. So how can you tell from this list that among these 73 persons charged with theft that none of them pertained to the operations or the actions on the 25th and 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind each and every one of these names there is a criminal report. There is a description of the incident, minutes compiled about items seized, and we can see from those where it happened. Mr. Cepic showed just a few examples, and I know that they were in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you read all those criminal reports related to these 132 entries?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before criminal reports were filed before a court, before they were sent to the court, I can't say I read them all, but I saw them all because the security officer who was dealing with that was duty-bound to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the most significant entries in here, I would say, is at item number 103 through 106. That concerns Major Mancic, the two privates, and a Captain Radojevic charged with war crimes against civilians. You're familiar with that particular event, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you testified in Milosevic, and perhaps here as well, that this was one that you didn't find out about right away. It only came to light I think late in the war or even after the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was just after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that those two privates, Tesic and Seregi, shot and killed two Albanian civilians that had been detained during an action they were engaged in. That's what it's about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they killed two civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I seem to recall from seeing some documents about that criminal proceeding that the allegation -- or the claim was they said that they had been ordered to kill those men by Major Mancic after those individuals had been questioned. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what those soldiers said. That case is being retried. I cannot -- I cannot speculate about this, because the case is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The case is still ongoing as to all four of these individuals, Major Mancic, the two privates, and Captain Radojevic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Supreme Court, as far as I know, quashed the verdict and returned it for a renewed procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was Major Mancic released from custody when that happened or even before that happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it correct that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I have already once objected to any comment being made about ongoing proceedings. There is a clear indication and the witness said himself that a trial is underway and any comment would be interference with the court and the case. The officer's duty is to file a criminal report, but any further comments would interfere with the independence and the work of judicial bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to pursue this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have one other question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you about some of the incidents alleged in the indictment. You testified about Bela Crkva, and you mentioned passing through Bela Crkva after the 25th of March I think up to the 4th of April? Is that correct? Did you also pass through on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said the 4th or the 5th. I passed on the 25th, 26th, and the 27th, up to the 4th, perhaps the 5th of April, and once again in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your testimony was that when you passed through on the 26th, 27th, and the 4th of April, and again in May, you saw no damage to Bela Crkva, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see anything that would be out of the ordinary in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P98. And, Your Honours, actually I'd like to make an oral application. This exhibit was originally shown to Mr. Riedlmayer when he testified. The version we have in e-court appears to have been scanned from a copy of something. It's not a very good copy. I have a hard copy here. We have a better copy of this that we would propose to put into e-court, with the leave of your Court and barring any objection by the Defence. Dr. Riedlmayer told us that this was something he had seen on the NATO web site, and that's where this comes from. You can probably see on the current version in e-court that it appears to be highly overexposed and is not very useful I would submit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have a copy of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Riedlmayer talked about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue then, Mr. Hannis, using the clearer version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I can hand a hard copy to the General if -- I'll assure the Defence has a hard copy of the same thing they're seeing on the left side of the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remove the poorer-quality one from the screen and expand the other one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a photograph purporting to show Bela Crkva. On the left side of your photo on the 11th of March, 1999, and in the centre of the photograph I understand that that's the mosque and the tall column there casting a shadow to the left and behind the building is the minaret to the mosque. Can you recognise that, even though it's an aerial photograph, can you recognise that as Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty that it's Bela Crkva. It could be any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you disagree with me if I told you it's Bela Crkva and it's been indicated as such by another witness in this case? I mean, do you have any reason to dispute it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to dispute it. If the picture were broader and if we could see the roads, then we could say really whether it's Bela Crkva or not. This way we can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we are also very confused with those two pictures. Are they representing the same site or not for the first because I don't see that they represent the same site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was an issue that may have arisen when they were originally exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was an explanation from Mr. Riedlmayer, Professor Riedlmayer, that the photograph on the right is actually rotated 180 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I tell you that, that the photograph on the right has the bend of the river on the right-hand side of the photograph. If you can in your mind rotate that photograph on the right 180 degrees, can you then see and understand that this is the same area that's depicted on the right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's probably the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does this photograph on the right dated the 2nd of April, 1999, not show extensive damage to buildings in Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing can be seen on this photograph. It's not a photograph that could serve as a basis for any analysis, because while the left-hand side photo is clear, the right-hand side is blurred as if it was all covered by fog. And to claim that the right-hand photo, especially rotated this way, I don't think this claim stands up to scrutiny. Again, let me ask, why is one photograph clear and the other absolutely not clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, Witness Professor Riedlmayer told us that on the right-hand photograph it appeared to him that the minaret to the mosque is no longer standing. Isn't it true that the mosque in Bela Crkva was damaged during that last week in March when your forces were going through that area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my forces were there, the mosque was standing throughout that time. Now based on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question relates to the minaret. Are you saying it was standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am saying the minaret was there while I was there. I can't say I looked at the minaret every day, but on the 25th when I was passing through the mosque and the minaret were intact. Now, based on this 2nd April photograph, nobody can claim that the minaret is missing because the photograph is simply blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, could you in the last minute remaining take a pen and mark on this screen where you would have driven through when you passed through Bela Crkva on the 4th or 5th of April. Would you have gone along one of these roads depicted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, the witness answered that he cannot recognise easy the Bela Crkva or some other village. His answer now -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've moved on from that point and he's capable of speaking for himself, but he knows now that the river is depicted. He can see roads in the left-hand one clearly in relation to both the river and the mosque. He's familiar with the location of the mosque in Bela Crkva, and should now be able to tell us whether he thinks this is Bela Crkva or not. And if he remains of the view that he can't tell, then he won't be able to assist us. What is the position, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that this is a very narrow photograph. You can see just some local roads, and I say, although I have no reason to doubt what the Prosecutor is saying I do not claim that this is Bela Crkva. This road cannot be seen here. I used the main road to get here -- to get there, the road from Prizren via Zrze to Orahovac, and if you look at another map you can see that road. Here on these photographs that road doesn't exist, it's just not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that you certainly did not pass close to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is Bela Crkva, I'm saying that I passed along a asphalt road. I didn't take any of the roads that can be seen on this photograph that is clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that answer doesn't -- I can't understand in English. You didn't take any of the roads that can be seen on this photograph at all; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- yes, that is what I said. I did not take any of the roads. These are local roads. I used the main road leading towards Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When passing, how close were you to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my opinion, the mosque may be some 300 or 500 metres away, so up to half a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the minaret visible when you passed? I don't mean was it there, but was it normally visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In normal conditions, it was visible, certainly, but I have to say now that I was not there to look at whether the minaret was there or not. This was something just in passing. I'm sure about that on the 25th, but I paid attention to the general picture. I didn't focus my attention on checking whether the mosque and the minaret were there every day, so I can't make any claims to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, that's where we must end for today, Mr. Delic. We need you back again tomorrow at 9.00, same place, and we will have a similar sitting arrangement, from 9.00 to 3.30. So could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I know that there's been some communications taking place in relation to translations. I'm not up-to-date with these, and therefore I'm not in a position to deal with that at this point in time, but they will be dealt with urgently. On the other matter, however, of the expert report, can you give us any more information?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The e-mail from the Senior Legal Officer, Grant Dawson, said that this should be taken care of prior to the winter recess, we are in the process of doing that, and it's my understanding that both the English and the B/C/S versions of the report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- will be amended or corrected with respect to the format that was discussed earlier in the week, that is to say prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful. All that needs to be done is upload them into e-court. Filing is not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That is what we will do then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We will adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.36 p.m.,
